summary.heading: Stage 1: Change is real, and cannot coherently be denied
summary.plain: Coffee cools, leaves fall, puddles grow, flies die — things change. An ancient Greek, Parmenides, argued that change is impossible, since it would mean something coming out of nothing. Feser’s first reply: you cannot even work through an argument against change without your own thoughts changing as you go. The proof starts from something nobody can coherently deny.
summary.body:
Four everyday examples, one for each kind of change Aristotelians recognize: coffee cooling (**qualitative**), a leaf falling (**local**, change of place), a puddle growing (**quantitative**), a swatted fly dying (**substantial**). Our senses report all four. And even if, as in Descartes or *The Matrix*, your whole life were a dream, one experience would still give way to the next — which is change.

**Parmenides**’ objection: the coffee’s coldness does not exist while the coffee is hot, so its coming to be would be something coming from nothing. Feser answers twice. The view is **self-refuting** — reasoning your way to it means moving from premise to premise, which is itself a change. And, as the next lesson shows, Aristotle denies that change requires anything to come from nothing.

Notice how little Feser is claiming. He does not need the senses to be reliable, or physics, or an external world. He needs only that one thought succeeds another. The starting point is deliberately more basic than any observation — which is why the objections from physics later in the chapter have trouble reaching it.
summary.takeaway: Change cannot coherently be denied — denying it is itself a change — so the argument’s first premise survives even radical doubt about the senses and the external world.
summary.deepDive:
Be precise about what the self-refutation reply proves. It shows that **change in the mind** is undeniable. It does not yet show that the external world changes, and Feser does not need it to: when he later answers the block-universe objection, he says that change existing *at least in the mind* is all the argument requires to get started. A deceived dreamer still undergoes a real succession of experiences.

Parmenides’ argument laid bare:

1. If the coffee becomes cold, coldness comes from what is not.
2. What is not is nothing, and nothing comes from nothing.
3. So the coffee cannot become cold.

The weak point is the assumption hidden in step 1 that there are only two options, full being and sheer nothing. Aristotle’s reply adds a third — being-in-potency. Parmenides was right that nothing comes from nothing; he was wrong that change requires it.

**Two things people get wrong here.** That the argument depends on trusting the senses — it does not, and Feser grants they might deceive us. And that ‘change’ means ‘motion through space’. For an Aristotelian, cooling, growing and dying are changes too, and all four kinds get the same analysis.

checks.q: What is Feser’s first reply to Parmenides’ argument that change is impossible?
options: Anyone reasoning to the conclusion that change is unreal is thereby undergoing change
Science has measured change directly
Parmenides misunderstood the physics of heat
Descartes proved that the senses are reliable
checks.explanation: Working through an argument from premises to conclusion is itself a change, so denying change presupposes it. Feser doesn’t rely on the reliability of the senses; he grants they might deceive us.

checks.q: Feser’s four opening examples — coffee cooling, a leaf falling, a puddle growing, a fly dying — are chosen to make what point?
options: That ‘change’ in this argument covers far more than motion through space
That the senses are reliable
That every change has a physical cause
That Parmenides used the same four examples
checks.explanation: They illustrate the four kinds of change: qualitative, local, quantitative and substantial. All four get the same act–potency analysis, so nothing later in the argument is about motion specifically.

checks.q: Why doesn’t the dream or *Matrix* scenario threaten the premise that change is real?
options: Dreams are too rare to matter
Even a dreamer’s experiences succeed one another, and that succession is change
Simulations must obey the laws of physics
Feser proves that we are not dreaming
checks.explanation: Feser grants the far-fetched scenario for argument’s sake; change in one’s thoughts and experiences would still occur.

summary.heading: Aristotle’s answer: actuality and potentiality
summary.plain: Before hot coffee turns cold, its coldness isn’t *nothing*. It is a real ‘can be’ in the coffee — coffee can go cold, but it cannot turn into a chicken. What a thing already is, philosophers call its **actuality**; what it can become, its **potentiality**. Change is a ‘can be’ becoming an ‘is’.
summary.body:
While the coffee is hot its coldness is not **actual** — but it is not nothing either, since it is there **potentially**. The coffee can cool, stain the rug, or wake you up; it cannot fuel an engine, turn into chicken soup, or become a live chicken. That it has some of these capacities and lacks others shows that potentiality is real and determinate, sitting between full actuality and sheer nothing. So change is **the actualization of a potential** — not something from nothing, because the potential was never nothing.

A thing’s potentials are rooted in what it actually is. Coffee can cool because it is actually a hot liquid, and can wake you because it actually contains caffeine. Potency is always the potency *of* something actual, and each thing carries a definite range of it.

Note the shape of the move. Aristotle does not reject Parmenides’ principle that nothing comes from nothing; he accepts it, and refines the analysis of change so that change no longer violates it. Feser says this is the pattern of the whole chapter: the jargon of act and potency does not contradict common sense, it lets us follow common sense out to its implications.
summary.takeaway: A potential is a real, specific capacity, not nothing — so change is the actualizing of a potential rather than something coming from nothing.
summary.deepDive:
Three cases side by side show that ‘a potential is not nothing’ is no verbal trick:

- **Actual coldness**: the coffee is cold.
- **Potential coldness**: the coffee is hot but *can* become cold.
- **No potential at all**: the coffee cannot become a live chicken, however long you wait.

The difference between the second and the third is a fact about the coffee, not about our imagination. That fact is what Aristotle calls potentiality.

Worked example: an acorn. It is *actually* an acorn — small, brown, hard. It is *potentially* an oak. It is not potentially a dog, a violin, or a sonnet. When it grows, nothing comes from nothing; a potential it always had is actualized.

A potential is not the same as a logical or imaginative possibility. A cartoon coffee cup can turn into a chicken, and there is no contradiction in the idea — but the coffee has no *potency* for it. Throughout the chapter, ‘potential’ means a real capacity in a real thing.

This is **step 2** of the formal argument, and it sets up **step 4**: precisely because a potential is not yet actual, it can do nothing on its own. It also foreshadows the conclusion — at one end, mere potential that cannot act; at the other, **pure actuality**, with no unrealized potential at all.

checks.q: Why does it matter that coffee can cool but cannot become chicken soup?
options: It shows coffee cannot really change at all
It proves the principle of causality directly
It shows a thing’s potentials are specific and real rather than nothing
It shows soup is more actual than coffee
checks.explanation: Having some potentials and lacking others shows potentiality is a determinate feature of the thing. That is why Aristotle can say the coffee’s coldness was ‘not nothing’ before it cooled.

checks.q: Does Aristotle accept Parmenides’ principle that something cannot come from nothing?
options: No, he rejects it as the source of Parmenides’ error
Yes. He agrees, and shows that change doesn’t require something to come from nothing
Only for substantial change
Only for material things
checks.explanation: Aristotle keeps the principle and denies the hidden assumption that what doesn’t actually exist is simply nothing.

summary.heading: Change requires a changer: the principle of causality
summary.plain: A ‘can be’ cannot turn itself into an ‘is’; something that already *is* has to do it — the cool air chills the coffee. That is the **principle of causality**. Read it carefully: it does not say ‘everything has a cause’. It says only that whatever goes from potential to actual needs something already actual to make that happen.
summary.body:
Every change has something that brings it about — the cool air chills the coffee, your wrist drives the swatter. But this is not a generalization from examples. It **follows from what change is**. The coffee’s coldness, while merely potential, can hardly do anything, precisely because only what is actual can act. So the potential cannot actualize itself; something already actual — the cool air, an ice cube — must do it.

1. A potential, as such, is not yet actual.
2. Only what is actual can do anything.
3. So a potential cannot actualize itself.
4. So whenever a potential is actualized, something already actual is doing the actualizing.

Two points of precision, both of which matter later. Feser calls the cause a ‘changer’ colloquially, but **actualizer** is the exact word, because the principle will shortly be applied where nothing changes over time at all — the desk actualizing the cup’s being three feet up, and ultimately whatever actualizes a thing’s very existence at a moment. And the principle’s subject is *what goes from potential to actual*. It says nothing whatever about something that has no potentials.
summary.takeaway: A mere potential cannot make itself actual, so whatever goes from potential to actual needs something already actual to actualize it — which is not the same as saying everything has a cause.
summary.deepDive:
Why is this a necessary principle rather than a well-confirmed rule of thumb? Compare ‘every swan is white’. That is learned by counting swans and refuted by one black swan. ‘No potential actualizes itself’ is also first noticed in experience, but its truth does not rest on the count.

Try to describe a counterexample in detail. The coffee’s potential coldness would have to *do* something — bring about actual coldness. But to do anything it would already have to be actual coldness, in which case the coffee is already cold, which is exactly what it isn’t. The counterexample dissolves. A critic cannot refute the principle by producing a puzzling case; he has to exhibit a merely potential feature bringing itself into actuality, which is what ‘merely potential’ rules out.

Three things the principle does **not** say, each of which gets mistaken for it somewhere in this chapter:

- Not ‘everything has a cause’. Only what passes from potency to act needs an actualizer. That one difference defuses ‘What caused God?’
- Not ‘every cause of change is itself changing’. Feser says explicitly that this does not follow and is not true.
- Not ‘the cause comes earlier in time’. The desk actualizes the cup’s height *now*.

And it is not **determinism**. The principle requires that the effect be brought about by something actual; it does not require that the cause necessitate the effect. Feser leans hard on that distinction when he answers the quantum objections.

Nearly every objection in the chapter — Hume, Kant, Russell, inertia, quantum mechanics, radioactive decay — is an attack on this principle (**step 4**) or on its scope.

checks.q: Why, according to Feser, is the principle of causality more than a generalization from examples?
options: It has been confirmed by every physics experiment
Aristotle observed it without exception
It is true by the dictionary definition of ‘cause’
It follows from what potentiality is: what is merely potential can’t do anything
checks.explanation: Feser grounds the principle in the nature of potency. Only the actual can act, so no potential can actualize itself. Observation confirms it but isn’t its foundation.

checks.q: Which statement is the principle of causality as Feser formulates it?
options: Whatever goes from potential to actual is actualized by something already actual
Every event is determined by earlier events
Everything that exists has a cause
Whatever begins to exist has a cause
checks.explanation: The principle concerns transitions from potency to act. The other options are, respectively, determinism, the straw man behind ‘What caused God?’, and the kalām argument’s premise.

checks.q: A critic says: ‘Quantum mechanics shows some events aren’t fixed by prior events, so the principle of causality is false.’ What has he assumed that the principle never claims?
options: That a cause must necessitate its effect
That every existing thing has a cause
That causes always precede their effects in time
That potentials are real features of things
checks.explanation: The principle requires only that something actual do the actualizing, not that it determine the outcome. Feser makes this the centre of his reply to the quantum objections.

summary.heading: Linear series stretching back in time
summary.plain: Causes often come in chains stretching back through time: you pressed the button, the air conditioner came on, the air cooled, the coffee cooled. Feser grants — for the sake of argument — that such a chain could run back forever, with no first moment and no beginning of the universe. His proof does not need one, so Big Bang debates do not touch it.
summary.body:
Often a changer is itself being changed: the air’s coolness was actualized by the air conditioner, your wrist’s motion by firing neurons. Feser is careful here. He does *not* claim that every changer must itself be changing — he says that does not follow and is not true. The claim is conditional: *if* a cause is changing, its change needs a cause of its own.

So we get series — coffee ← air ← air conditioner ← your finger on the button — running **backward in time**, in a **linear** way. Feser then grants that such a series might be **infinite**, with no first member, as Aristotle himself believed. Many assume the Big Bang settles this; some scientists speculate about a prior universe that imploded, or a beginningless series of universes. Feser calls the speculation dubious and then says it **does not matter**: the argument works either way.

The concession costs nothing because of what a linear series is. Once a member is in place it acts on its own power relative to the others — the air conditioner keeps cooling the room after you leave the house or drop dead. Nothing in such a series demands a first member.
summary.takeaway: Feser grants that a chain of causes through time might have no beginning. The argument does not depend on the universe having started.
summary.deepDive:
Picture dominoes stretching back forever, each falling because the one before struck it. There is no contradiction in every domino having a predecessor. The important feature is that once a domino is falling it does not need the earlier one to keep existing or keep pushing. That is the mark of a linear series: each member, once in place, has its own causal power *relative to the other members*. Feser’s footnote example works the same way — Al begets Bob, Bob begets Chuck, and Bob can beget whether or not Al is still alive.

Why is Feser so careful about ‘every changer is itself changing’? Because if that were true, an unchanging first cause would be ruled out by definition and the argument could not reach its own conclusion. Keeping the claim conditional leaves room for a cause that actualizes without being actualized.

Now look at the fifty-step statement and notice what is missing: no step mentions the past, a first moment, or a beginning. **Steps 6–13** all concern what is required ‘at any given moment’. The linear series appears in the chapter only in order to be set aside.

**Two things people get wrong.** Assuming every cosmological argument is a Big Bang or **kalām** argument (‘whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist’). And assuming every infinite regress is vicious — Aristotelians happily allow a beginningless linear series. The vicious kind involves borrowed power, and it is what comes next.

checks.q: Why does Feser say it doesn’t matter whether the Big Bang was the absolute beginning of everything?
options: Because the Big Bang theory has been refuted
Because the argument concerns what sustains things now, not a first moment in time
Because the multiverse has been proven to exist
Because Aristotle already proved the world began
checks.explanation: Feser grants a possibly beginningless universe or multiverse. The argument rests on hierarchical series operating at every moment, not on a first moment.

checks.q: Which claim does Feser explicitly NOT make?
options: Some causes of change are themselves being changed
If a changer is itself changing, its change needs a changer
Every changer must itself be undergoing change
Series of changes often extend backward in time
checks.explanation: He says this doesn’t follow and isn’t true. Keeping the claim conditional is what leaves room for an unchanging first actualizer.

summary.heading: The hierarchical series: cup, desk, floor, earth
summary.plain: There is a second kind of chain, one that works all at once. Your cup stays three feet up because the desk holds it *right now*, the desk because the floor holds it right now, and so on down to the earth. None of the middle items has any holding power of its own; each passes along support it is receiving this instant, the way a paintbrush paints only because a painter is moving it. Let the floor go and desk and cup go with it.
summary.body:
The second kind of series is easiest to introduce by looking at a single moment — though, as Feser insists, being simultaneous is not what makes it what it is. Your cup is three feet up because the desk holds it *now*; the desk is held *now* by the floor, the floor by the foundation, the foundation by the earth. A lamp hangs from a chain, held by a fixture, held by the ceiling, held by the walls, all at once. Each step is an actualized potential — the desk actualizes the cup’s potential to be three feet off the ground — with no passage of time involved.

What makes such a series **hierarchical** is the **dependence** of the later members on the earlier ones *for the very power in question*. The cup cannot stay up on its own. Neither can the desk: it would fall to the earth without the floor, and the floor holds the desk only because the foundation holds the floor. So in a real sense it is the earth holding up the cup, **through intermediaries** that act as **instruments** — as it is the painter, not the brush, who paints. Compare the linear case: switch on the air conditioner and it keeps cooling after you leave. But let the floor collapse and the desk stops holding the cup at that moment.

One of Feser’s series traces downward to the ground, the other upward to the ceiling. Direction is irrelevant; dependence is the whole point.
summary.takeaway: In a hierarchical series every later member acts only while, and because, an earlier member is acting through it. Its causal power is borrowed, like a brush’s power in a painter’s hand.
summary.deepDive:
**Derivative** or **instrumental** causal power is the idea to get exactly right, because everything later in the chapter turns on it.

Start with the brush. The brush really does something — it carries the pigment and lays down the stroke. But it contributes no power *of its own*. Set the painter aside and the brush lies still. That is what ‘derived’ means: it acts only insofar as something else is acting through it, right now.

A test for sorting the two kinds of series: **if the earlier member stopped acting this instant, would the later member’s causal activity stop this instant?**

- You stop pressing the button; the air conditioner keeps cooling. → linear
- The floor collapses; the desk stops holding the cup at once. → hierarchical
- Your hand stops moving the stick; the stick stops pushing the stone. → hierarchical

Work one out yourself. In a mechanical watch, the mainspring drives a gear, which drives another, which turns the hands. Every gear turns only while it is being turned. Not one of them has any power of its own to move the hands — and adding gears never produces any.

Two refinements Feser insists on. First, simultaneity is the way *in* to the idea, not its definition; what defines the series is the later members’ dependence for the power at issue. (He returns to this when answering the objection that simultaneous causes do not exist.) Second, an intermediate member may have plenty of features of its own — the desk is rigid, the chain is strong — and still have no independent power to do *the particular thing in question*, which is holding the cup at that height. Rigidity with nothing underneath it holds nothing up.

Why does this matter so much? Because the conclusion of the whole proof is not ‘something started it all’ but ‘something is holding it all up’. **Step 11** — that a regress of concurrent actualizers cannot be infinite — is a claim about series of this kind and no other.

checks.q: Which test best distinguishes a hierarchical series from a linear one?
options: Whether its members are in the same place
Whether it has finitely many members
Whether it involves living things
Whether a later member’s activity would cease at once if an earlier member stopped acting
checks.explanation: In a hierarchical series, later members act only while being acted on (floor collapses → cup falls). In a linear series they carry on (the air conditioner keeps running after you leave).

checks.q: In Feser’s analogy, the desk, floor and walls are to the earth as…
options: the brush is to the painter
the son is to the father
the air conditioner is to you after you’ve left
an effect is to its past cause
checks.explanation: They are instruments through which the earth holds up the cup and the lamp, as the painter paints through the brush. The father–son relation is Feser’s linear example.

checks.q: In this chapter, calling a causal series ‘hierarchical’ means that it is ordered by…
options: importance or rank
size, from largest to smallest
the dependence of later members on earlier ones for the very power at issue
time, from earliest to latest
checks.explanation: The word has nothing to do with rank or scale, and simultaneity is only a way into the idea. Dependence for the power in question is what defines it.

summary.heading: What ‘first’ means
summary.plain: In an all-at-once chain, something has to be the actual source of the power the others pass along. ‘First’ here does not mean ‘earliest’, and it does not mean ‘at the head of the queue’. It means: has the power built in instead of borrowing it. A paintbrush cannot move itself, and an infinitely long handle would not help.
summary.body:
A hierarchical series needs a first member — but not first in time. Since the intermediaries have no power of their own to hold anything up, the series could not exist at all unless something could hold them up **without being held up itself**. If they are acting as instruments, something must be using them; if their power is borrowed, something must have it ‘built in’. A first cause in this sense is one whose causal power is **nonderivative and noninstrumental** — able to actualize without itself being actualized.

Finitude is not the point either. A paintbrush cannot move itself, and an **infinitely long handle** would not change that; an infinite stack of desks would be exactly as powerless to hold up the cup as one desk. Three senses of ‘first’ need separating:

- **Temporally first** — the earliest event, whatever happened at the Big Bang.
- **Numerically first** — the one that comes before the second, third and fourth.
- **Primary** — the source of underived causal power, from which the rest borrow.

Feser means only the third. The question is never ‘how many members are there?’ but ‘where does the power come from?’ He also drops a hint he will collect later: even the earth is not a first cause in the strict sense.
summary.takeaway: A ‘first’ cause in a hierarchical series is first because its causal power is underived — not because it comes earliest, and not because the series is short.
summary.deepDive:
Why would an infinite series of instruments be exactly as powerless as a single one?

Suppose A borrows $100 from B, B borrows it from C, C from D, and so on. If *everyone* in the chain is only a borrower — nobody has the money except by having borrowed it — then no loan ever happens. Lengthening the chain does not conjure the money into being. Somewhere there has to be someone who has it without borrowing it.

Feser’s own images make the point. An infinitely long brush handle still cannot move itself, because wood has no built-in power of motion and more wood adds none. An infinite stack of desks holds up the cup no better than one desk, because each is powerless alone and infinitely many powerless things are still powerless. The need for a first member comes from the **derived character of the power**, not from anything problematic about infinity — which is why Feser can say ‘even if there could be such a thing’. He never has to argue that an actual infinity is impossible, and the argument is stronger for not depending on contested mathematics.

The tempting reply is: ‘If every member is explained by the one before it, then every member is explained.’ What that explains is each member’s *passing the power along*. The power itself is never explained. Explaining one borrowing by another borrowing, forever, never says where the money came from.

Notice, finally, that Feser’s definition of a first cause — something that can actualize a potential without itself having to be actualized — is already the idea of an **uncaused cause**, at least with respect to the power at issue. Applied to the existence of things, it yields the unactualized actualizer.

This is **steps 10–12**: the regress either runs forever or terminates in pure act, and step 11 rejects the first option.

checks.q: Which sense of ‘first’ is relevant to Feser’s argument?
options: Earliest in time
At the head of a finite queue
Having causal power in a built-in, underived way
Largest or most impressive member
checks.explanation: Feser means ‘primary’ as opposed to ‘secondary’ or derivative, not first in time or first in a count.

checks.q: What does Feser say about an infinite stack of desks?
options: It could hold up the cup, since each desk is held by the next
Without something outside it, it would be as powerless to hold the cup as a single desk
It is impossible, since infinity is contradictory
It would be a linear series
checks.explanation: Each desk lacks the power on its own, and adding more such desks, even infinitely many, supplies none. Feser doesn’t argue that infinity is impossible.

checks.q: A friend says: ‘If every member is held up by the one below, forever, then everything is explained.’ What is missing?
options: Any account of where the holding-up power comes from at all
A beginning in time
A proof that infinity is impossible
A scientific measurement of the forces
checks.explanation: Each member only transmits power it receives, so the infinite chain explains the transmissions but never the source of the power.

summary.heading: Taking stock: the hierarchical series is more fundamental
summary.plain: A pause to sum up. Chains through time — the first kind — might run back forever. But every link in such a chain depends, at every moment it acts, on an all-at-once chain of the second kind. So the second kind is the deeper one. The traditional names: *per accidens* (through time) and *per se* (all at once).
summary.body:
In a linear series each member has its own causal power relative to the others: the air stays cool and keeps chilling the coffee for a while even after the air conditioner is off. In a hierarchical series every member but the first has only **derivative** power. The hierarchical kind is harder to see, because it requires taking the idea of actualizing a potential — first introduced to explain change over time — and applying it where the passage of time is not essential. But it is **more fundamental**: every linear series presupposes hierarchical ones, which trace down to a first cause, and, Feser adds pointedly, to a *single* first cause. A footnote supplies the scholastic labels: linear = ordered **per accidens**, hierarchical = ordered **per se**.

Why more fundamental? Because every member of a linear series has to exist at the moment it acts, and its existing at that moment depends on hierarchical series.
summary.takeaway: Every linear series of causes through time rests on hierarchical series operating at each moment, which makes the hierarchical kind the more fundamental.
summary.deepDive:
Draw it. A horizontal line of events: you press the button → the air conditioner runs → the air cools → the coffee cools. Now hang a vertical column beneath each point on that line. At the moment the air conditioner is cooling the air, the air conditioner has to exist — and its existing *as an air conditioner* right now depends on its parts holding together as they do, which depends on their molecular structure, which depends on atoms and particles, all at that same moment. The same goes for the air and for the coffee. Every horizontal link sits on a vertical stack.

Feser’s Al–Bob–Chuck footnote makes the same point about people. Each man can beget a son on his own power relative to the others; yet none of them could beget, or do anything else, for an instant unless the matter of his body were being actualized here and now as a living human body — which is in nobody’s power.

So you can remove the earlier horizontal links — leave the house, die — and the air conditioner keeps running. You cannot remove the vertical stack beneath it for an instant without the air conditioner ceasing to exist at all.

Note that *per accidens* does not mean ‘random’. It means the ordering is not essential to each member’s present causal activity.

This is the bridge from **step 5** to **steps 6–7** (every change presupposes a substance, whose existence at each moment itself needs actualizing), and it is why **step 13** can say that the occurrence of *any* change presupposes a purely actual actualizer.

**A common misreading:** that the chapter offers two arguments, one about the past and one about the present. It offers one. The linear series is introduced so that it can be set aside.

checks.q: Why are hierarchical series more fundamental than linear ones?
options: Hierarchical series are always longer
Linear series are illusions
Hierarchical series were discovered first
Every member of a linear series exists, whenever it acts, only through hierarchical series operating at that moment
checks.explanation: Things can change or cause change only if they exist, and their existence at each moment depends on hierarchical series. Hence the Al–Bob–Chuck footnote.

checks.q: What does ‘per accidens’ mean in ‘a series ordered per accidens’?
options: The series happens by chance
The ordering is not essential to each member’s causal activity
The members are accidents rather than substances
The series is irrational
checks.explanation: Each member can act on its own power relative to the others, so the ordering is incidental rather than essential to the causal activity. It doesn’t mean ‘random’.

summary.heading: From change to existence: what keeps the coffee in being right now?
summary.plain: Here is the pivot of the whole proof. Forget how your coffee was made: what keeps it existing *right now*? Its water exists only because its matter is, this instant, holding together as water rather than as separate hydrogen and oxygen. That depends on atoms, which depend on particles — an all-at-once chain of dependence, not for where the coffee is, but for its existing at all. Answers about the past or the future do not touch the question.
summary.body:
Coffee can cool, or be held up by the desk, only if it **exists**. So: what makes it exist — not how it was brewed, but what keeps it in being here and now, at any particular moment that it exists?

Take the water that makes up the bulk of it. That matter also has the potential to exist instead as separate quantities of hydrogen and oxygen. That is not the potential being actualized right now; its potential to exist *as water* is. Why? Three answers suggest themselves, and each answers a different question:

- *A past process combined the gases.* That tells us **how the water got here**.
- *Nothing has come along to split it.* That tells us **how it might someday cease to be**.
- *Chemical bonding.* That **restates** the question, since the atoms have the potential to be bonded in other ways and are not.

Appealing to atomic structure only pushes the question down a level: why are the subatomic particles combined in just this way, here and now, rather than another?

This is the cup on the desk all over again — except that what is at stake is the thing’s **existence**, not merely its location. The coffee’s existing depends on the water’s, the water’s on an actualized potential of its atoms, theirs on one of their particles. That is a **hierarchical series of actualizers of existence**, and so, by the last two lessons, it must have a first member. And the reasoning covers anything with the potential either to exist or not to exist — which is every material thing.
summary.takeaway: A thing’s existing right now is itself an actualized potential, so it needs an actualizer right now. That opens a hierarchical series whose members actualize *existence*.
summary.deepDive:
Why should a thing’s merely existing at a moment count as an actualized potential? This is the single hardest claim in the chapter, and the rest of the proof rests on it.

Start from a general pattern that has nothing to do with God. Whenever something has several potentials and only one of them is realized, we can ask what is making *that* one actual. The matter in your glass has more than one: it could exist as liquid water, or as separate quantities of hydrogen and oxygen. Right now one of them is actual — it exists *as water*. So ‘what is actualizing that potential, at this instant?’ is an ordinary question, of exactly the kind we asked about the cup’s being three feet up.

Freeze time at a single instant to feel the force of it. Inside a single instant, ‘what caused this?’ in the sense of ‘what came before?’ has no application at all. But ‘what makes this matter be water rather than separate gases, at this instant?’ still makes complete sense. That is Feser’s question, and it is why the argument never needs time to pass.

Now watch why the natural answers miss. *The past reaction* and *nothing has split it* are answers about the two ends of the thing’s career — how it started, how it might finish. Neither says anything about the middle, about now. *Chemical bonding* and *atomic structure* are not answers at all but relocations of the question: the atoms could be bonded otherwise, so why this way, now? — and the same question arises again one level down.

The deepest resistance usually takes this form: **‘Things just persist by default. Nothing has to keep them in existence; they continue unless something destroys them.’** That is the second failed answer wearing a suit. It tells you what would end the water’s existence. It does not tell you what makes its matter constitute water rather than separate gases at this moment. Feser’s claim is that persistence is not a null state requiring nothing, because at every moment one potential among several is the one being realized.

A caution about the example. Feser notes in a footnote that talking about the water’s atoms makes the water sound like a mere aggregate of them; on the Aristotelian **hylemorphic** view the atoms exist in the water only ‘virtually’, and its real constituents are substantial form and prime matter. He deliberately avoids that machinery, because the argument does not need it. Either way, the water does not explain itself.

This secures **step 7** (the existence of a substance at any moment presupposes the concurrent actualization of its potential for existence) and therefore **step 8** (every substance has, at each moment, an actualizer of its existence).

checks.q: According to Feser, which answer explains only how the water might cease to exist, not what keeps it in existence?
options: Nothing has yet come along to separate the hydrogen and oxygen
A past chemical process combined the gases
The atoms’ potential to form water is being actualized now
A purely actual actualizer sustains it
checks.explanation: Pointing out that nothing has broken the water up concerns its possible destruction. A past reaction explains how it came to be. Neither answers the question about the present.

checks.q: Why doesn’t appealing to atomic structure settle the question of what keeps the water in existence?
options: Atoms don’t really exist
Atomic theory is outdated
It pushes the same question down a level: why are the particles arranged this way now?
It concerns only the past
checks.explanation: Every lower level has potentials of its own being actualized, so we get a hierarchical series rather than an answer.

checks.q: A friend replies: ‘Nothing has to keep the water in existence — things just persist unless something destroys them.’ Which of Feser’s failed answers is this, restated?
options: The appeal to the past reaction that produced the water
The appeal to the fact that nothing has yet split the water apart
The appeal to chemical bonding
The appeal to atomic structure
checks.explanation: It tells us what would end the water’s existence, not what makes its matter constitute water rather than separate gases at this instant.

summary.heading: The unactualized actualizer
summary.plain: So there must be something at the bottom that keeps everything else in existence without needing anything to keep it in existence. It has no ‘can be’ left over — only ‘is’. Philosophers call that **pure actuality**; Aristotle called it the Unmoved Mover. It is not something that merely happens to have no cause. It is the sort of thing that could not need one.
summary.body:
The first member must actualize the existence of other things **without its own existence needing actualization**. So it has no potential for existence at all. It does not merely *have* actuality, the way the things it sustains do; it **is pure actuality**. And it does not merely happen to lack a cause: it could not in principle have had or needed one, because there is nothing in it that could need actualizing. It is an **uncaused cause** — Aristotle’s **Unmoved Mover**, or, more precisely, an **unactualized actualizer**.

The route began not with the universe but with a cup of coffee. The result is nevertheless universal: every material thing — the leaf, the fly, anything with the potential either to exist or not — can exist at any moment only if certain potentials are being actualized, and so only because an unactualized actualizer is causing it to exist.

A footnote adds the hylemorphic version. Water is not an aggregate of atoms; its metaphysical constituents are **substantial form** and **prime matter**, each depending on the other for its concrete existence. That mutual dependence would be an explanatory circle unless something outside the composite were keeping it in being.
summary.takeaway: The first member of a series of actualizers of existence must have no potential for existence at all — pure actuality, an unactualized actualizer that could not even in principle have a cause.
summary.deepDive:
The move from ‘first actualizer of existence’ to **pure actuality** is worth slowing down.

Everything in ordinary experience *has* actuality, mixed with potentiality. The water is actually water and potentially separate gases; the atom is actually bonded this way and potentially otherwise. Feser’s conclusion is that the first actualizer does not merely have actuality alongside some potentials: there is nothing merely potential in it at all.

Run the test on any candidate. Suppose the bottom of the hierarchy were some fundamental field or particle. Does it have any potential for existence — any way it could fail to exist, or exist otherwise? If so, its existing now is an actualized potential, and by **step 4** it needs an actualizer, so it was not the bottom after all. Only something with no potential for existence needing actualization can stop the regress — and nothing in such a thing could have needed a cause.

Two things to keep straight.

Strictly, this section establishes that the first actualizer has no potential *for existence*. That it has no potential *at all* — that it is purely actual in every respect — is nailed down at the very end of the chapter, in the three-way dilemma of ‘Why an unmovable mover?’

And the universal conclusion is reached without any premise about the universe. The argument starts with a cup of coffee and applies to every material thing only because every material thing is, in the relevant respect, like the coffee.

**Two misreadings.** Hearing ‘uncaused’ as ‘brute fact’ or ‘random’ — pure actuality is uncaused not because it is inexplicable but because there is nothing in it to be caused. And hearing it as ‘self-caused’ — nothing can cause itself, and Feser never says this one does.

**Steps 12–14**: either the actualizer is purely actual, or the regress it begins ends in something that is; so a purely actual actualizer exists.

checks.q: Why couldn’t the unactualized actualizer have needed a cause, even in principle?
options: It is too powerful to be caused
It has no potential that could be actualized
It existed before time
Causes apply only to material things
checks.explanation: Things need causes because they have potentials to be actualized. What is purely actual has none, so a cause would have nothing to do.

checks.q: Where does Feser’s route to the unactualized actualizer begin?
options: With the universe as a whole
With the Big Bang
With the concept of God
With ordinary individual things like a cup of coffee
checks.explanation: He emphasizes that the argument doesn’t start from the universe as a whole. Its universal scope is a consequence of applying the reasoning to each material thing.

summary.heading: Stage 2: Why call it God? Immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal
summary.plain: Why call this source ‘God’? Two reasons. It is what keeps everything in existence at every moment — and whatever else God is supposed to be, he is the ultimate cause of things. And the traditional divine attributes follow from having no ‘can be’ at all: it cannot change; what cannot change is not in time; and what is not in time and cannot change is not physical.
summary.body:
Stage 2 argues that the undeniable reality of change entails the existence of **God**. Feser gives a sketch here and promises a full chapter later.

- **Immutable**: change is the actualization of a potential, and there is no potential here to actualize.
- **Eternal**: existing within time entails changeability, so it exists **outside time** altogether, neither coming to be nor passing away.
- **Immaterial**: being material entails being changeable and existing within time.
- **Incorporeal**: having a body of any sort means being material.

Read each as a claim about *capacity*, not activity. **Step 22** says that if the purely actual actualizer existed in time it *would be capable of* change — not that it would in fact be changing.

These are ‘negative’ attributes: they say what the first cause is not. They are nonetheless decisive, because they rule out every physical candidate for the role — a field, energy, the laws of physics, the universe itself — each of which is changeable and temporal.
summary.takeaway: No potential means no change; no change means no time; no change and no time mean no matter and no body. The negative attributes follow almost immediately from pure actuality.
summary.deepDive:
The one link worth dwelling on is between being **in time** and being **changeable**.

Take a stone that has sat untouched in a field for a year. It has not changed in any obvious way. Is it still in time? Yes — and notice why. It has a past and a future; it could be moved, cracked, weathered. It is *capable* of change even while not changing. To exist in time is to exist through a succession of moments, and passing through that succession is itself a passage from potency to act. So what cannot change is not in time at all.

That gives **eternity** in a strong sense: not ‘very old’, not ‘existing at every moment of an endless time’, but existing outside the succession of moments altogether.

Then **matter**. Whatever is material — water, stone, star, field — can take on different arrangements, states and locations. That is a large part of what being material is. What has no potency can have none of it.

**Three ways this gets misheard.** ‘Eternal’ as infinitely long duration (no: timeless). ‘Immaterial’ as made of some fine invisible stuff, like energy (no: energy is physical and changeable). ‘Immutable’ as inert or frozen (no: the immutable cause is the source of all activity — unchanging because it lacks nothing, not because it does nothing).

**Steps 19–21** (immutability), **22–23** (eternity), **24–25** (immateriality), **26–27** (incorporeality).

checks.q: Why must an immutable cause exist outside time?
options: Because time began at the Big Bang
Because it has existed for infinitely long
Because existing in time entails being capable of change
Because only material things decay
checks.explanation: Step 22: what is in time is capable of change. Pure act isn’t, so it is timeless. The cosmological history of time is irrelevant.

checks.q: Which is the correct understanding of divine eternity in this chapter?
options: Existing outside time altogether, without beginning, end or succession
Existing at every moment of an endless time
Existing before the universe began
Existing for an extremely long time
checks.explanation: Feser’s eternity is timelessness, not everlasting duration within time.

summary.heading: Perfection, goodness and unity
summary.plain: To be imperfect is to be missing something your nature calls for — like an injured squirrel that can no longer outrun predators. Philosophers call such a lack a **privation**. Something with no unrealized ‘can be’ lacks nothing, so it is perfect; and since being good, in the broad sense, is being fully what you are meant to be, it is fully good. That also settles how many there can be: telling two things apart requires one to have something the other lacks, and here there is nothing to lack.
summary.body:
A squirrel hit by a car may be unable to outrun predators; a tree with damaged roots may be unstable or starved of water. Such a defect is a **privation** — the absence of some feature a thing’s nature requires, a failure to realize a potential inherent in it. A thing is perfect to the extent that it has realized such potentials and is free of privation. So what is purely actual has **maximal perfection**.

**Goodness**, in the broad sense, works the same way: a thing is good to the extent that it realizes the potentials inherent in it as the kind of thing it is, and bad to the extent that it fails. A good painter has mastered craftsmanship and composition; a bad one has not acquired the skills. A purely actual cause can be deficient in no way, so it is **fully good**.

Two clarifications before the payoff. A privation is not just any absence — a squirrel lacks wings, but that is no defect, because nothing about being a squirrel calls for wings. Imperfection is always measured against a thing’s own nature. And ‘good’ here is the broad metaphysical sense in which we speak of a good knife or a good eye, not the moral sense; God and evil come in a later chapter.

Now **unity**. Could there be more than one purely actual cause? Not even in principle. Two things of a kind need some **differentiating** feature. We normally distinguish things by material or temporal features — larger, taller, earlier — but what is purely actual is immaterial and eternal. More generally, things of a kind differ by some perfection or privation that one has and the other lacks: sturdier roots, a missing tail. But what is purely actual lacks nothing and is maximal in perfection. So there is no way even in principle to make two of them two. There is exactly **one** unactualized actualizer, and everything that exists owes its existence to it.
summary.takeaway: Imperfection and badness are privations — potentials a thing’s nature calls for and has not realized. Pure actuality has none, so it is perfect and fully good; and since any difference between two such beings would be a privation in one of them, there can be only one.
summary.deepDive:
**Goodness as actualization.** It sounds odd until you listen to ordinary speech. We call a knife good if it cuts well, an eye good if it sees clearly, a heart good if it pumps efficiently, a painter good if he has mastered his craft. In each case the standard comes from *the kind of thing it is*. A knife is for cutting, so a dull knife is a bad knife — not because we dislike it, but because it falls short of what a knife is. Badness in this sense is a gap between what a thing is and what its nature calls for, and a gap like that is an unrealized potential: a **privation**.

Now imagine something with no such gap anywhere — no capacity left unrealized, nothing it ought to have and lacks. It could not be defective in any respect. That is not being good *at* something, the way a painter is good at painting. It is perfection without qualification.

**Why two of a kind need a difference.** Two coins come off the same press one after the other. They look identical, yet they are two, and we can always say what distinguishes them: different places, a scratch on one, a second’s difference in age. Now strip away every such difference — same place, same time, same features, same history, same everything. What would make them two? Nothing. You would have described one coin twice.

Apply that to pure actuality. The usual differentiators come in two families, and both are unavailable. **Material and temporal** features — size, shape, location, earlier and later — require materiality and temporality, which pure act lacks. **Perfections and privations** — one has what the other lacks — require that the one lacking it have an unrealized potential, which pure act cannot have.

A wrinkle worth noticing. Feser’s informal version of the unity argument leans on immateriality and eternity, but the formal statement puts unity *first*, at **steps 15–18**, before those attributes are derived — and there it rests on the single premise that any differentiating feature would require an unactualized potential in one of them. That is the premise a critic has to attack.

**Two things this is not.** It is not divine **simplicity** (the claim that God has no parts at all), which is a separate attribute defended elsewhere in the book. And it does not merely make many gods unlikely: any god limited to a domain would have unrealized potential, and so would not be purely actual in the first place.

**Steps 28–29** (perfection), **30–32** (goodness) and **15–18** (unity), all resting on **step 20**, that pure actuality has no unactualized potential. Unity matters downstream too: **step 34** speaks of *the* purely actual actualizer from which all power derives, and **step 39** of *the* cause of all things.

checks.q: According to Feser, what is a privation?
options: The absence of a feature a thing’s nature requires for completeness
Any absence of any feature whatsoever
A moral wrong committed by a person
One of a thing’s potentials
checks.explanation: A privation is a lack measured against what a thing’s nature calls for. A squirrel lacking wings has no privation; a squirrel unable to run after an accident does.

checks.q: In the chapter’s broad sense of ‘good’, why is a knife that won’t cut a bad knife?
options: Because people dislike dull knives
Because it is made of matter
Because it was produced long ago
Because it fails to realize what a knife’s nature calls for
checks.explanation: Goodness in this sense means realizing the potentials proper to one’s kind, like Feser’s good and bad painters. Moral goodness is a later chapter’s topic.

checks.q: Why can’t two purely actual beings differ by one having a perfection the other lacks?
options: Perfections can’t be counted
Both would then have to be material
The one lacking the perfection would have an unrealized potential, so it wouldn’t be purely actual
Perfections belong only to living things
checks.explanation: Lacking a perfection means having an unactualized potential, which contradicts pure actuality. That is the heart of step 16.

summary.heading: Omnipotence
summary.plain: Power is the ability to make something happen. Every power anything has is ultimately received from this one source, the way a brush’s power to paint comes from the painter. And the source is not one powerful thing among others with a fixed supply; nothing limits it. That is what ‘omnipotent’ means here.
summary.body:
To have **power** is just to be able to make something happen — to actualize some potential. The purely actual cause is not merely one actual thing among others but pure actuality itself, and it is the source of all the actualizing power anything else has. So it has all possible power: it is **omnipotent**.

Why ‘all possible power’ rather than ‘a very great deal’? Two things do the work. Stage 1 showed that everything with potentials — which is every cause we meet — exists and acts only because its potentials are being actualized, here and now, by a series terminating in pure actuality. So every power anything has is ultimately derived from that source. And the source is not a limited thing with a fixed quantity of power, like a very strong engine; being pure actuality, it is not limited by any potency at all. Nothing caps it.

None of this makes ordinary causes fake. The desk really does hold up the cup; its power is real, just not underived.
summary.takeaway: All actualizing power derives from the purely actual actualizer, and nothing limits it, so it is omnipotent.
summary.deepDive:
A power station supplies every appliance in a city — toasters, trains, hospitals — so in a sense all the electrical power in the city is the station’s. The analogy gets you the first half of the argument and then breaks, usefully. A power station has a finite capacity and can run short. Pure actuality is not a store of power at all; it is actuality unlimited by potency. Being the source of all power, in its case, is having every power there could be.

Note what ‘power’ means here. Feser defines it as the ability to actualize a potential, which covers heating, pushing, holding up, bonding, begetting. Physical force and energy are particular ways of making things happen, not the general notion.

**Two misreadings.** ‘Omnipotent means able to do anything at all, even make square circles’ — power is the ability to actualize potentials, and a contradiction is nobody’s potential. And ‘if all power comes from God, creatures do nothing’ — the brush really paints, and it paints *because* the painter moves it. Derived causation is genuine causation.

**Steps 33–37.**

checks.q: What does Feser mean by ‘power’ in the omnipotence argument?
options: Physical force, as measured in newtons
The authority to command obedience
The ability to do anything imaginable, including contradictions
The ability to make something happen, that is, to actualize some potential
checks.explanation: Step 33: to have power is to be able to actualize potentials. Force and energy are particular cases of that.

checks.q: If all power derives from the purely actual actualizer, what follows about ordinary causes like the desk holding the cup?
options: They do nothing; only the first cause really acts
Their causal power is real but derived, as a brush really paints in a painter’s hand
They are illusions produced by our senses
They have power entirely independent of any source
checks.explanation: Derivative causation is still genuine causation. This is the instrumental picture from the cup-and-desk example, not a denial that secondary causes act.

summary.heading: What intelligence is
summary.plain: What is intelligence, at root? The ability to grasp general ideas — the idea of *triangle*, which covers every possible triangle — and then to combine them into thoughts and reason with them. Having the idea of a triangle means having a triangle’s pattern in your mind without your mind being a triangle. That is the capacity the next two lessons will go looking for in the first cause.
summary.body:
Intelligence, as traditionally understood, involves three capacities: grasping **universal concepts** (the concept *man*, which applies to every possible man, not only actual ones); combining them into complete **thoughts** (*all men are mortal*); and **reasoning** from thought to thought (*so Socrates is mortal*). The first is the most fundamental, since thoughts are built out of concepts and inferences out of thoughts.

To have a concept is to have in the mind the same **form or pattern** that exists in the things you think about. When that form comes to exist in matter, the result is an individual — this man, this triangle. When a mind grasps it, it is had in a universal way, abstracted from every particular. That is the essence of strictly intellectual activity: **having the form of a thing without being that kind of thing**. A material triangle *is* a triangle; you think triangularity without becoming one.

So there are two ways for a form to exist — concretely, in individual things, and abstractly, in an intellect. That contrast does all the work in the derivation two lessons from now.
summary.takeaway: The heart of intelligence is grasping universal forms: having the form of a thing without being that kind of thing.
summary.deepDive:
Picture a triangle. Your mental image has some size, some particular shape, perhaps a colour. Now ask whether your *concept* of triangle has a size. It does not. It covers huge and tiny triangles, right-angled and obtuse, triangles drawn in ink and triangles in no material at all. So the concept is not the image. It is your grasp of the pattern all triangles share — a closed plane figure with three straight sides. Understood, that pattern is ‘in’ your mind universally; in a drawn triangle the very same pattern is realized in a particular bit of matter.

This is also why **imagination and intellect are different powers**. Imagination traffics in particular images, intellect in universal concepts. You can understand a thousand-sided figure perfectly well while being unable to picture one distinctly.

The universality matters for what is coming. Your concept *man* applies to all *possible* men, not merely those that exist or have existed — and Feser will argue that the cause of *every possible* thing must have the forms of things in exactly that unrestricted way.

**A modern confusion:** equating intelligence with processing speed or problem-solving, as in ‘artificial intelligence’. The traditional notion is about grasping universals.

**Step 41** (forms exist either concretely in things or abstractly in an intellect) and **steps 43–44** depend on this lesson.

checks.q: Why does Feser treat grasping universal concepts as the most fundamental of the three capacities of intellect?
options: Because it is the hardest of the three
Because thoughts are built out of concepts, and inferences out of thoughts
Because only human beings have it
Because concepts are stored in the brain
checks.explanation: You couldn’t form complete thoughts or reason from one to another without the concepts that are their constituents.

checks.q: What, according to Feser, is the essence of strictly intellectual activity?
options: Processing information quickly
Having the form or pattern of a thing without being that kind of thing
Forming vivid mental images
Perceiving particular objects through the senses
checks.explanation: A material triangle has triangularity by being a triangle; a mind has it without being one. Images and perception concern particulars.

summary.heading: The principle of proportionate causality: the $20 gift
summary.plain: A cause cannot give what it does not have in any way. If I give you $20, I must have it somehow — as cash, as credit in the bank, or through some higher power to produce twenties in the first place. The traditional names for those three ways are **formally**, **virtually** and **eminently**. What is in the effect must be in the cause, though not necessarily in the same form.
summary.body:
Alongside the principle of causality stands the **principle of proportionate causality**: whatever is in an effect must in some way or other be in its cause, even if not in the same way — because a cause cannot give what it does not have to give.

I can give you $20 only if I have it somehow: a twenty or smaller bills in my wallet; $20 in the bank to write a cheque against; the ability to borrow or earn it; or, fancifully, an act of Congress licensing me to print my own twenties. If none of these is available to me, I cannot do it. Feser’s three traditional modes:

- **Formally** — I have the bill in hand. I already instantiate the pattern I cause you to instantiate.
- **Virtually** — I lack the bill but have the power to get it: the bank balance.
- **Eminently** — I have the higher power to make twenties exist in the first place: the printing licence.

So what is in an effect must be in its cause at least virtually or eminently, even if not formally.

Notice how tightly this is bound to the principle of causality. Both rest on the insight that only what is actual can act. The first says a potential needs something actual to actualize it; the second says the actualizer can communicate only actuality it somehow possesses.
summary.takeaway: A cause cannot give what it does not have, so whatever is in an effect is in its cause — formally, virtually, or eminently.
summary.deepDive:
Work the three modes with your own examples.

- **Formally**: a teacher who knows calculus teaches you calculus. The very thing you acquire is in her in the same form — Feser’s bill in the wallet.
- **Virtually**: a student who does not know the answer but has the textbook and the skill to look it up has the answer virtually. She has the power to get it — the bank balance.
- **Eminently**: a novelist who invents a character has that character in a *higher* way than the character has anything at all. She is the source of its existence, not a copy of it — the printing licence.

In each case the reality of the effect is **accounted for** by something in the cause. What is ruled out is an effect containing more than its cause can account for — handing you $20 with no money, no credit, and no power to get or make any.

**The standard misreading** is that a cause must resemble its effect: that a cause of red things must be red, or a cause of material things material. Only the *formal* mode involves sameness. When Feser applies the principle to the purely actual cause, he says the effects are in it virtually and eminently, *not* formally: it is not a cat, and being immaterial cannot be one — but it has, in a higher way, the power to make cats exist.

This is **step 38**, which with **step 39** yields **step 40**: the forms of all things are somehow in the purely actual actualizer. Everything said about intelligence and omniscience rests on it.

checks.q: Having authority to print your own $20 bills illustrates having the effect in the cause…
options: formally
virtually
eminently
accidentally
checks.explanation: It is the higher power to bring such things into existence at all. A bill in hand is formal; bank credit is virtual.

checks.q: Which of the following does the principle of proportionate causality NOT require?
options: That the cause possess the effect’s feature in exactly the same way the effect does
That a cause somehow possess what it gives
That a cause cannot give what it lacks
That the effect’s reality be accounted for by the cause
checks.explanation: Only the formal mode involves sameness. Virtual and eminent possession are enough, which is why the cause of cats needn’t be a cat.

checks.q: How does the principle of proportionate causality relate to the principle of causality?
options: They are the same principle stated twice
The first contradicts the second
The principle of causality is derived from it
The principle of causality says an actualizer is needed; this one says what the actualizer must somehow contain
checks.explanation: Both rest on the idea that only the actual can act, but they answer different questions.

summary.heading: Intelligence and omniscience derived
summary.plain: Put the last two lessons together. The source causes every kind of thing there is or could be — cats, trees, stones — so by the last lesson’s principle it must somehow contain the patterns of all of them. It cannot contain them by *being* a cat or a tree, since it is not physical. The only other way a pattern can be contained is the way a mind contains an idea. So it is intelligent — and since nothing that could exist falls outside those ideas, it knows everything.
summary.body:
The purely actual cause is the cause of **everything that exists or could exist**. And to cause a thing to exist is always to cause something *of a particular sort* — a stone rather than a tree, a tree rather than a cat — that is, something having a certain **form**. So it is the cause of every possible form; and by proportionate causality, those forms must be in it. They must be in it in a completely **universal or abstract** way, since it is the cause of every possible thing fitting each form. But to have forms in that universal way is precisely the capacity fundamental to **intellect**.

It is also the cause of the **relations** among things: not only of men but of the fact that all men are mortal; not only of this cat but of this cat’s being on this mat. So these too must exist in it, as combinations of forms — which is how **thoughts** exist in us. What exists in things pre-exists in their cause, Feser says, in something like the way the things we make pre-exist as ideas or plans in our minds: **virtually and eminently**, not formally.

And since nothing that exists or could exist lies outside the range of those thoughts, the cause is **omniscient**.

Notice what sort of argument this is not. It is not a design argument. It does not infer a designer from order or complexity in nature. It runs entirely on the metaphysics of what it takes to cause a thing’s *existence*.
summary.takeaway: The cause of all things must contain the forms of everything it causes, and the only way it can contain them is the way an intellect contains ideas. So it is intelligent — and omniscient, since nothing possible escapes those ideas.
summary.deepDive:
The derivation in six small steps:

1. To cause something to exist is always to cause a thing *of some kind* — a stone rather than a tree. That is, a thing with a certain form.
2. By proportionate causality, whatever is in the effect must be in the cause in some way. So the forms of things are in their cause.
3. A form can exist in exactly two ways: **concretely**, as the form of this particular cat, or **abstractly**, as in a mind that grasps *cat* in general.
4. It cannot be in the purely actual cause concretely — that cause is immaterial and one, and is not a cat and a tree and a stone.
5. It causes *every possible* cat, not just this one, so it must have the form in a way not tied to any particular instance: universally.
6. Having forms universally, without being the things that have them, is what intellect is. So the cause is intelligent.

The premise doing the most work is step 3 — that concretely and abstractly exhaust the ways a form can exist. That is **step 41** of the formal argument, and it is where a critic should press.

Then **relations**. The cause accounts not only for cats and mats but for *this cat’s being on this mat*; not only for men but for *all men being mortal*. Relations are combinations of forms, and combinations of forms are exactly what thoughts are. So the effects exist in the cause the way an architect’s plan for a house exists in her mind before the house does — as a pattern she could realize in many houses. The purely actual cause is like that for everything that exists or could exist, with the forms present eminently rather than as one more thing among things.

Feser is speaking **analogically** throughout: the forms are there ‘virtually and eminently’, and the effects exist in the cause ‘in something like’ the way thoughts exist in us. How such language applies to God is taken up in the chapter on God’s nature.

**Three misreadings.** That this is the design argument (it starts from causing existence, not from apparent design, and would go through in a universe that looked chaotic). That it makes God a giant brain (intellect is having forms universally, which requires no organ). That a God with ideas of all things must have parts (that worry belongs to divine simplicity, defended elsewhere).

**Steps 38–47.**

checks.q: Why can’t the forms of things exist in pure actuality the way they exist in individual things?
options: Because it is immaterial and cannot itself be a cat or a tree
Because forms don’t really exist
Because God is too distant from the world
Because forms exist only in human minds
checks.explanation: Step 42. Pure act is immaterial and one, and it causes every possible instance, so it must have the forms universally, as an intellect does.

checks.q: What shows that the purely actual cause’s thoughts include relations among things, and not just kinds of things?
options: That it is immutable
That it is eternal
That it is one
That it causes how things are related, such as this cat’s being on this mat
checks.explanation: Since it causes relations too, these must pre-exist in it as combinations of forms, the way thoughts exist in us.

checks.q: Why is this not a design argument?
options: Because it infers a designer from the complexity of living things
Because it starts from what it takes to cause a thing to exist, not from order or complexity in nature
Because it concerns only the origin of the universe
Because it never mentions God
checks.explanation: Design arguments reason from observed order to a designer. This one reasons from the metaphysics of causing existence, via proportionate causality.

summary.heading: The formal statement: a 50-step argument
summary.plain: Feser now restates the whole case as fifty short numbered steps. Steps 1–14 take you from ‘things change’ to ‘there is a purely actual source’; steps 15–50 show that this source has the traits of God. The value of the list is that it makes disagreement precise: you can point at the step you reject.
summary.body:
After a brief recap, Feser restates the case in fifty steps (the Argument tab has every one):

- **1–14**: change; the principle of causality; the move from a change to the existence, at that moment, of the thing that changes; a hierarchical regress of concurrent actualizers that cannot be infinite — therefore a purely actual actualizer.
- **15–18** unity; **19–27** immutability, eternity, immateriality, incorporeality; **28–32** perfection and goodness; **33–37** omnipotence; **38–47** intelligence and omniscience, via proportionate causality.
- **48–50**: such a cause is just what it is for God to exist; so God exists.

Most of the fifty are inferences or definitions. The **premises** — the claims that have to be defended independently — are few: an observation (step 1); analyses of what change and existence involve (2, 6, 7, 41); two causal principles (4, 38); exhaustive disjunctions (9, 41); the regress claim (11); and definitions (36, 46, 49).

Notice what is *not* among the premises: that the universe had a beginning, that everything has a cause, or that the universe as a whole needs a cause. The useful habit when meeting an objection is to ask which numbered step it targets. Often the answer is ‘none’.
summary.takeaway: Stage 1 (steps 1–14) proves that a purely actual actualizer exists; Stage 2 (15–50) derives the divine attributes from pure actuality. The numbering adds no content — it makes the structure checkable.
summary.deepDive:
Match each objection in the chapter to the step it actually targets:

- ‘The universe may be eternal.’ → **no step**; no premise mentions a beginning.
- ‘Parts have causes, but not the whole.’ → **no step**; the premises quantify over ‘any substance S’.
- ‘What caused God?’ → a misreading of **step 4**, which concerns only what goes from potential to actual.
- Hume (uncaused beginnings are conceivable) → **step 4**.
- Kant (causal reasoning stops at experience) → the *scope* of **step 4**.
- Russell, inertia, quantum mechanics, radioactive decay → **step 4**, or **step 1** via ‘change is unreal’.
- The block universe → **step 1** — though **step 7** shows the argument survives without step 1 anyway.
- ‘There are no simultaneous causes’; infinite series; the question-begging charge → **step 11**.
- ‘Unmoved but not unmovable’ → **steps 12–14**, and so **step 20**.

Two things fall out of the exercise. The premises are far more modest than people assume; and nearly the whole battle is over **step 4** (the principle of causality), **step 7** (existence at a moment involves actualized potential) and **step 11** (no infinite hierarchical regress). Every objection section in the rest of the chapter is a defence of one of those three.

The argument can also be assessed **in stages**: someone could accept Stage 1 and still dispute a particular attribute derivation, and Feser concedes that Stage 2 is a sketch to be defended more fully later.

**A misleading intuition:** that a long argument must be weaker, because more can go wrong. The length here comes from making every inference explicit, which makes the argument easier to check, not harder.

checks.q: The objection ‘The universe may be eternal’ targets which step of the formal argument?
options: Step 1
Step 7
Step 11
None, since no step says the universe had a beginning
checks.explanation: The premises concern what is required at any given moment. The age of the universe appears nowhere in them.

checks.q: Which description of the fifty steps is accurate?
options: All fifty are independent assumptions that must be separately defended
Most are inferences or definitions; the premises needing independent defence are few
None of them are premises
They are all empirical claims about the physical world
checks.explanation: The load falls on a handful of premises — above all steps 4, 7 and 11. ‘Fifty steps’ does not mean ‘fifty assumptions’.

summary.heading: Three misreadings: a beginning, the whole universe, and ‘What caused God?’
summary.plain: Three objections come up constantly, and all three attack premises the argument never had. *It assumes the universe had a beginning* — it doesn’t; Feser allows that the universe may have existed forever. *It assumes the universe as a whole needs a cause* — it doesn’t; it starts from a single cup of coffee. *If everything needs a cause, what caused God?* — the argument never says everything needs a cause. It says that things with unrealized ‘can be’s need something to make them real, and the source has none.
summary.body:
Feser first grants that the derivation of the divine attributes rests on assumptions that are bound to be controversial, to be defended later — but notes that even the sketch already shows how weak the stock complaint is that first-cause arguments cannot tell you enough about their cause to call it God. Objections to first-cause arguments in general wait for a later chapter; this section takes on those aimed at the specifically Aristotelian features, beginning with three misreadings.

**‘It assumes a beginning.’** Readers are so used to arguments for God framed in terms of a first moment that they read the framing into an argument that explicitly denies it, and then ask how we can be so sure the universe really did have a beginning. But what Feser said is that an infinite past is **irrelevant**. The claim is that for things to exist here and now, and at any moment at which they exist, they must be **sustained** in existence.

**‘It assumes the whole universe needs a cause.’** No premise concerns the universe as a whole. The argument starts with **any single thing** — a stone, a cup of coffee. That it then applies to everything is a **consequence** of the argument, not a premise of it.

**‘What caused God? Isn’t that special pleading?’** The argument never says everything has a cause; it says that **whatever goes from potential to actual** does. And the exemption is not arbitrary: things need causes *because* they have potentialities needing actualization, and what is purely actual has none, so it neither needs nor could have a cause. To insist there is no significant difference between the two principles, Feser says, is like insisting there is no significant difference between ‘all triangles have three sides’ and ‘all geometrical figures have three sides’.

To the follow-up that the potential-to-actual formulation is an **ad hoc** dodge, he answers three times. Motives do not refute claims — that is **ad hominem**. The charge is historically false: for more than 2,300 years, from Aristotle to Aquinas to the present, the principle has been stated this way. And the formulation follows naturally from Aristotle’s analysis of change, independently of any argument about God — one hardly needs to believe in God to find it implausible that something merely potential could actualize itself.
summary.takeaway: None of the three objections touches a premise the argument actually has. It concerns what sustains any single thing right now, and it exempts pure actuality for exactly the reason the causal principle holds in the first place.
summary.deepDive:
**Why ‘everything needs a sustaining cause’ is a consequence, not a fallacy of composition.** Compare two inferences:

- *Composition (fallacious)*: each brick in the wall is light, so the wall is light. This infers a property of the **whole** from properties of its **parts**.
- *Distributive (fine)*: each person in this room needs oxygen right now, so everyone in the room needs oxygen right now. This restates, for all of them together, what is true of each one.

The Aristotelian argument is the second kind. Take a stone: it exists now only because its minerals’ potential to constitute a stone is being actualized, which depends on molecules, atoms and particles, and the series ends in pure act. Now take a leaf, a fly, a star — same reasoning, same result. The claim about ‘everything’ just collects the individual results. At no point do we reason from parts to whole. You can see this in **steps 6–8**, which speak of ‘any substance S’.

**Why the exemption for God is principled.** A rule says: anyone who borrows a library book must return it. Someone objects: then the library must return its books too!
