But the rule’s rationale is *borrowing* — it applies to borrowers because they hold what belongs to another. The library is not exempted by fiat; it falls outside the rule because it does not borrow. Likewise the principle of causality applies to things *because* they have potentials needing actualization. What has no potential falls outside it for precisely the reason the principle holds.

That also answers the natural follow-up, ‘then why not say the universe is uncaused?’ Because the universe is changing all the time and is therefore full of potentiality. The exemption is available only to what is purely actual — which is not a menu of candidates but exactly one.

And if someone insists the first cause *did* have a cause, that cause would itself have to be purely actual, or the regress would simply continue. ‘What caused the first cause?’ is really a request to run **step 11** again.

**Two things Feser is not saying.** That God is *self*-caused — pure act is *uncaused*, and nothing can cause itself. And that anything at all might turn out to be uncaused — only what lacks potency could be.

**The persistent confusion** is with the **kalām** argument (‘whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist’), which does depend on a beginning. Feser’s argument would go through even if the kalām argument failed completely.

checks.q: What does Feser say about the claim that the universe as a whole has a cause?
options: It is a premise of the argument
It is false
It is a consequence of the argument, not a premise
It requires the Big Bang to be true
checks.explanation: The argument starts from any single object; applying it to everything is a result of the reasoning, not an assumption. Hence no fallacy of composition.

checks.q: Feser’s triangle comparison responds to which claim?
options: That God is triangular
That there’s no real difference between ‘whatever goes from potential to actual has a cause’ and ‘everything has a cause’
That geometry proves God exists
That the universe is shaped like a triangle
checks.explanation: Equating the two principles is like equating ‘all triangles have three sides’ with ‘all geometrical figures have three sides’. Squares are not special pleading against the first.

checks.q: Which is NOT one of Feser’s replies to the charge that the potential-to-actual formulation is ad hoc?
options: The charge commits an ad hominem fallacy
The charge is historically false
The principle follows from the analysis of change
The formulation was introduced by Aquinas to answer Hume
checks.explanation: Aquinas lived centuries before Hume. Feser’s historical point is that the formulation goes back to Aristotle and has always been stated this way.

summary.heading: Hume and Kant on causation
summary.plain: David Hume said we can imagine something popping into existence with no cause. Feser replies that imagining a thing appear without picturing its cause is not the same as picturing it as having no cause — and that experience overwhelmingly supports the principle, since things do not in fact pop into existence. Immanuel Kant said the principle holds only inside experience; Feser answers that the *reason* it holds — a ‘can be’ cannot make itself real — has nothing to do with being observed.
summary.body:
**Hume.** Feser gives three replies.

- Imagining a stone or a coffee cup suddenly appearing in an empty space is conceiving it **without also conceiving its cause**, not conceiving it **as having none**. We can conceive of a trilateral without thinking ‘triangle’, or of a man without any thought of his height; neither could exist without the other.
- **Anscombe’s** point: what makes the appearance a *coming into existence* rather than a *transport* from somewhere else? Only the kind of cause involved — moulding a bit of porcelain versus picking a cup up and moving it. Spelling the scenario out in the detail Hume needs brings causation back in.
- Experience strongly **confirms** the principle. We find causes when we look for them, and when we do not find them — an unsolved murder — we still have reason to think they are there. As W. Norris Clarke puts it, were the principle false, an elephant or a hotel could appear on your front lawn out of nowhere, and it should be the easiest thing in the world for them to be popping up all the time. The best explanation of a world that does not behave that way is that potentiality by its very nature requires actualization by something already actual.

**Kant.** Why extend a principle learned from experience to something unobservable? Because the reason we conclude that things need causes is not *that we experience them* but *that they are merely potential until made actual* — and that principle is completely general. We learn Euclidean geometry from diagrams drawn in black ink, yet what we learn applies to figures of any colour and of no colour at all.
summary.takeaway: Imagining something appear without picturing its cause is not conceiving it as uncaused; and the causal principle applies wherever there is potentiality, observed or not.
summary.deepDive:
The whole Hume reply turns on one distinction: **conceiving A without conceiving B** versus **conceiving A existing without B**.

You can think about a number without thinking about whether it is prime — but every number is one or the other. You can think about a man without thinking about his height — but no man exists without some height. In each case, leaving B out of the thought is not the same as thinking of A as lacking B.

Now Hume’s stone. You picture empty space, then a stone. Have you conceived the stone *as having no cause*? No — you have simply not included a cause in the picture. Your thought is silent about the cause; it does not represent the cause as absent. Hold on to that distinction: it comes back, in a much sharper form, in the reply to quantum mechanics.

Anscombe’s point cuts deeper. What makes your picture one of a stone *coming into existence* rather than a stone being carried in from off-stage? Nothing in the bare image settles it. The only way to fix which scenario you mean is to specify the kind of cause — being made versus being moved. So the supposedly cause-free scenario cannot even be described without causal notions. Feser notes the irony, too: an empiricist ends up doubting one of the best-supported principles experience has ever given us.

Against **Kant**, the reply does not require refuting Kant’s system. It only locates the real ground of the principle. If things needed causes *because we perceive them*, the restriction to experience would follow. They need causes because they are merely potential until actualized — which is true of anything potential, seen or unseen. To think otherwise, Feser says, is like thinking Euclidean geometry applies only to figures we can see.

**A frequent overstatement:** that Hume *proved* causation is nothing but habit or constant conjunction. Feser’s claim here is narrower — his famous scenario does not establish what it is taken to establish.

**Step 4** and its scope.

checks.q: What key flaw does Feser find in Hume’s conceivability argument?
options: Conceiving of A without conceiving of B is not the same as conceiving of A existing without B
Hume couldn’t really imagine stones
Imagination always reflects reality accurately
Hume confused space with time
checks.explanation: Imagining the stone appearing leaves its cause out of the picture; it doesn’t picture the stone as uncaused (compare the trilateral and the triangle).

checks.q: On Feser’s reply to Kant, why does the principle of causality apply beyond experience?
options: Because we can experience God directly
Because Kant was secretly an empiricist
Because things need causes because they are potential, not because we experience them
Because geometry is purely empirical
checks.explanation: The ground of the principle is the nature of potentiality, which isn’t limited to observable things. Hence the Euclidean geometry comparison.

checks.q: How does Clarke’s elephant-and-hotel point support the principle of causality?
options: By proving that elephants need parents
By noting that if it were false, things should be popping into existence all the time, yet they don’t
By citing a law of physics
By appealing to intuition alone
checks.explanation: It is an inference to the best explanation. The world’s actual orderliness would be miraculous if potentials could actualize themselves.

summary.heading: Russell on causation
summary.plain: Bertrand Russell argued that physics contains only equations relating events, with no ‘causes’ anywhere in them, so causation is a relic of a bygone age. But physics deliberately describes only what can be put into mathematics — like a metal detector that finds only metal. Its silence about causes shows no more than a metal detector’s silence shows there is no wood. The later Russell admitted as much himself.
summary.body:
Russell’s claim: physics describes the world with differential equations relating events, and these make no reference to causes — ‘in the motions of mutually gravitating bodies, there is merely a formula’. Feser gives four replies.

1. **It proves too much.** ‘Event’, ‘law’ and ‘explanation’ are not in the equations either. As Jonathan Schaffer puts it, the argument is like claiming that mathematics has eliminated the variable, since the word ‘variable’ never appears in an equation.
2. **Physics is not obviously free of causal notions.** C. B. Martin argues that the fundamental particles described by physics clearly have **dispositional properties** — tendencies to produce certain effects when they interact in certain ways.
3. **Other sciences use causation** — biology, the social sciences, arguably chemistry — and are not reducible to physics. And naturalists themselves routinely rely on causal theories of knowledge, perception and meaning.
4. **Most basically: physics is not exhaustive.** The later Russell conceded that physics gives only the abstract logical structure of events, leaving their intrinsic character ‘completely unknown’ — silent about what it is that changes, and what it changes from and to.

Something must make the world run on these equations rather than on some others, or none. And if what the equations describe really is change, then it is the actualization of a potential — which is just what causing is.
summary.takeaway: Causes are missing from the equations of physics because physics’ mathematical method abstracts from them, not because causes aren’t real.
summary.deepDive:
The fourth reply is the deep one, and worth separating from the anti-science claim it gets mistaken for.

Begin with the later Russell’s distinction between **structure** and **intrinsic nature**. An equation tells you how measurable quantities relate — double this and that quadruples. It does not tell you what the things are that have those quantities, or, in Russell’s words, what it is that changes and what it changes from and to. A company’s spreadsheet can be perfectly accurate about revenues, costs and growth rates and say nothing about what the employees are like or why they do what they do. Accurate and partial are entirely compatible.

Physics achieves its precision *by* restricting itself to what can be described mathematically — Martin’s ‘partial consideration’. That restriction is a choice of method, and it cuts both ways. Whatever can be mathematicized, physics has an excellent chance of finding. Whatever cannot, physics is *guaranteed* not to find. So its silence about causes, potentials and intrinsic natures carries no evidential weight at all. Feser offers three images: the metal detector that never finds wood; the student who takes only courses he knows he will ace and concludes there is nothing worth learning elsewhere; the drunk searching for his keys under the lamppost because that is where the light is.

Even a thoroughgoing sceptic about mind-independent causation does not escape. The experience of setting up an experiment gives way to the experience of observing the result — that is change, and so actualization of potential. And, as the later Russell also granted, we know the physical world at all only because it has causal effects on our sense organs.

**The inference to watch for:** ‘if it isn’t in physics, it isn’t real.’ That is **scientism**, a philosophical thesis that science itself cannot establish.

checks.q: What is Jonathan Schaffer’s point against Russell, as Feser uses it?
options: Physics secretly contains causes
Russell’s argument proves too much: terms like ‘law’, ‘event’ and ‘variable’ don’t appear in equations either
Mathematics is useless for metaphysics
Causation is an illusion after all
checks.explanation: If absence from the equations proved unreality, science’s own indispensable concepts would be eliminated too, like claiming math has eliminated the variable.

checks.q: Which of his replies to Russell does Feser call the most basic?
options: That other sciences use causal notions
That particles have dispositional properties
That naturalists rely on causal theories
That physics doesn’t give an exhaustive description of reality
checks.explanation: The deepest problem is that physics abstracts from everything that can’t be mathematicized, so its silence about causes proves nothing either way.

summary.heading: Newton on inertia
summary.plain: Newton’s first law says a body in motion stays in motion unless an outside force acts on it. Doesn’t that show change without a cause? Feser answers that the argument is not about motion over time but about what makes a thing *exist* at a given moment — and that a law of nature describes how a thing with a certain nature behaves, so it presupposes that such things exist and cannot explain why they do.
summary.body:
Three replies to the objection from inertia.

1. **It answers a different question.** What Newton’s law describes are events ordered in time. The argument is concerned with what actualizes a thing’s potential to **exist** at any particular moment — with what makes it the case, right now, that these components actually constitute a water molecule rather than something else. Since Newton’s law presupposes things like water molecules, it can hardly explain their existence.
2. **Laws presuppose natures.** For something to follow a physical law is just for it to be the kind of thing that behaves that way; talk of a ‘law of nature’ is shorthand for how a thing will tend to operate given its nature or form. So: what makes it the case that there are things with *that* nature, governed by the law of inertia rather than some alternative law? Mechanics cannot say.
3. **Mathematical abstraction.** Following James Weisheipl, Feser argues that the mathematical science of nature does not prove the principle of inertia but **assumes** it, and must, if it is to remain mathematical. To equate quantities the mathematician has to treat some factors as carrying no quantitative value — motion, rest, constancy, unaltered direction — so that only *changes* in these have equational value. For the physicist, then, what needs explaining is change and cessation of motion, not motion’s continuation. Newton did not answer the question of a cause; he disregarded it and looked for two quantities he could equate.

So inertia does not refute the principle of causality — and on Feser’s account it could not, since mathematical physics can neither affirm nor deny causal realities. However inertia is interpreted, it has to be made compatible with the principle. A footnote offers one way of doing that: Aquinas held that a substance can manifest some motions **‘spontaneously’**, simply following from its nature, with no continuously conjoined external mover — their efficient cause being whatever generated the substance in the first place. Aquinas tied this to natural places, which are scientifically obsolete, but the general idea is separable from them, and some contemporary Aristotelians read inertial motion exactly this way.
summary.takeaway: Newton’s first law describes how things of a certain nature behave over time. It presupposes the existence of such things and so cannot explain it — and nothing in it exhibits a potential actualizing itself.
summary.deepDive:
Weisheipl’s claim — that mathematical physics **assumes** inertia rather than proving it — is the part worth working through.

Think about what an equation needs. To equate quantities you must hold something fixed as the baseline: the ‘nothing is happening here’ against which change is measured. In Newtonian mechanics the baseline is rest and uniform straight-line motion. Only *changes* in motion get quantitative value and show up as the effects of forces. So within the formalism, ‘what needs explaining’ just means ‘change of motion’. That is a fact about the representation, not a discovery that uniform motion has no cause of any kind.

A bank statement records only changes to your balance — deposits and withdrawals. A month with no entries does not mean your money existed without a bank holding it; it means nothing happened that the statement was designed to record. Inertia’s ‘no force needed’ says what the equations record, not what keeps the moving body in being.

**Two frequent errors.** That Aristotelians believe every moving object needs something continuously pushing it — Feser notes this was true of only some medieval Aristotelians, never the tradition as a whole. And that ‘no force required’ means ‘no cause required’ — force is one kind of cause among others, and the question this argument asks is about existence, not force.

checks.q: What is Feser’s first reply to the objection from inertia?
options: Inertia concerns events in time, but the argument concerns what actualizes a thing’s existence at a moment
The law of inertia is false
Newton was himself a theist
Motion is an illusion
checks.explanation: Newton’s law presupposes the existence of things like water molecules, so it can’t explain what makes them exist as such right now.

checks.q: According to Feser’s footnote, how do some contemporary Aristotelians interpret inertial motion?
options: As caused by angels pushing bodies
As entirely uncaused
As the way a body tends to move given its nature or substantial form
As proof of the block universe
checks.explanation: Following Aquinas’ idea of ‘spontaneous’ natural motion, but dropping natural places, inertia describes how a body behaves given its nature. Its efficient cause is whatever generated the body.

summary.heading: Einstein and the block universe
summary.plain: On one construal of relativity — Minkowski’s four-dimensional ‘block universe’ — past and future are as real as the present, the way distant places are as real as nearby ones, so nothing is ever actualized and change is an illusion. Feser doesn’t have to settle that dispute. Scientists get their evidence through experiences that succeed one another, so change cannot be wholly unreal — and even a frozen, changeless block would still need something to make it exist.
summary.body:
On the **block universe** model Hermann Minkowski built on relativity, time is analogous to space: just as distant places are as actual as nearby ones, past and future moments are as actual as the present. So there is no actualization of potential, and our experience of time passing is a feature of consciousness only. Feser notes that such claims are controversial even among physicists, and then declines to settle the controversy, because the argument survives either way.

1. **Denying all change is incoherent.** Physics, relativity included, rests on the empirical evidence of observation and experiment: formulating a prediction, then performing an observation to test it; moving from ignorance to knowledge. All of that involves change. So if there were no change, there would be no experiences to serve as evidence for any theory in whose name someone denies change. As Richard Healey argues, the view that physics shows all change to be illusory is incoherent. The most that could coherently be claimed is that change exists in the mind but not in mind-independent reality — and change in the mind is still actualization of potential, which is all the argument needs.
2. **Existence still needs actualizing.** Even granting no change anywhere, a thing’s very **existence** involves the actualization of a potential. The sheer existence of a four-dimensional block — in a single timeless moment, as it were — would require a cause of *that sort* of world being actual rather than some other sort. The same goes for the mind: even a changeless mind would need a cause of its being actual at all.

So relativity affects at most **how** the principle of causality is applied, not **whether** it applies.
summary.takeaway: Even if the block universe were true, change would remain in our experience, and the block’s own existence would still require an actualizer distinct from it.
summary.deepDive:
Why would a block universe with no change in it at all still require an actualizer? Because the pivot of Stage 1 was never about change.

Recall the change-to-existence lesson. Actualization of potential is not only what happens when things change over time; it is present in a thing’s very existing at any moment — the matter in your glass could be water or separate gases, and its being water now is an actualized potential. That analysis never required time to pass, which is exactly why it survives here.

Apply it to the block. Picture the whole four-dimensional universe as one timeless whole with nothing in it becoming anything. You can still ask why *this* block is actual, with these laws and these contents, rather than some other, or none. And it cannot be what actualizes its own potential, by **step 4**. So there must be an actualizer distinct from the world itself.

The first reply, meanwhile, is the Parmenides move again: a theory cannot coherently be used to abolish the very transitions — predict, then observe — that supply its own evidence.

**Two overstatements to resist.** ‘Einstein proved time is an illusion’ — the block universe is one interpretation of relativity, and a disputed one; Feser points to Lee Smolin on the other side. And ‘if the future is already real, nothing needs a cause’ — real or not, the whole still has to be actual rather than not.

**Step 1** (reply 1), and **steps 7–14** (reply 2), which go through even if step 1 were surrendered entirely.

checks.q: According to Feser’s use of Healey, what is the most that could coherently be claimed?
options: That no change exists anywhere at all
That time flows faster for people who think harder
That relativity theory is false
That change exists only in the mind, not in mind-independent reality
checks.explanation: Denying all change undermines the experiential evidence for physics; restricting change to the mind still leaves actualization of potential, which is enough for the argument.

checks.q: Why would even a changeless block universe still need an actualizer?
options: Because it began at the Big Bang
Because its very existence as this world rather than another involves actualized potential
Because relativity requires a first cause
Because observers need light to see it
checks.explanation: Existence at any moment — or timelessly — involves actualized potential. That is the shift from change to existence made in Stage 1.

summary.heading: Quantum mechanics: indeterminism, Bell, the vacuum
summary.plain: Quantum physics is said to embarrass the causal principle three ways: some events are genuinely random, distant measurements are correlated with no apparent common cause, and particles appear and vanish in ‘empty’ space. Feser’s replies: random is not the same as uncaused, because a cause has to make its effect *intelligible*, not guarantee it; and since the mathematics of physics leaves causes out by design, a cause’s absence from the equations is no evidence that there isn’t one.
summary.body:
Three objections. **Indeterminism**: the nondeterministic character of quantum systems. **Bell inequalities**: correlations between measurements made at distant locations that appear to have no common cause. **The quantum vacuum**: particles apparently coming into and going out of existence at random.

On indeterminism, it is sometimes pointed out that the de Broglie–Bohm hidden-variable interpretation lets quantum systems be seen as deterministic. But the deeper reply is that from an Aristotelian point of view it is a mistake to think **causality entails determinism** in the first place. For a cause to be sufficient to explain its effect it need not necessitate it; it need only make the effect **intelligible**. As Robert Koons notes, even on the Copenhagen interpretation every transition of a system has causal antecedents — the preceding quantum wave state, or that state plus the observation in the case of wave-packet collapse. On Bell, various responses have been proposed: allowing causal influences faster than light, backward causation, an absolute reference frame, or a law to the effect that the correlations occur. On the vacuum, Alexander Pruss suggests a hidden-variable theory, or that the system described by quantum field theory causes the events indeterministically. Feser bets on none of these, granting that interpreting quantum mechanics is a notoriously vexed business.

The deeper point is the one already used against Newton. Mathematical physics leaves causal content out by method, so a theory’s failing to assign a cause does not entail that there isn’t one. **The absence of something from a representation is not a representation of its absence.** A black-and-white drawing does not show that the scene has no colour.

Feser then goes further: quantum theory may, if anything, **point toward** the Aristotelian view. In comic art, a ‘colour hold’ leaves some contours to be supplied by the colour rather than the ink — and a viewer can often infer from the inked lines where the missing contours must go. Heisenberg compared the statistical expectations of quantum theory to Aristotle’s *potentia*. And quantum laws, like all laws, presuppose things with natures whose existence still needs actualizing.
summary.takeaway: Causation need not be deterministic, and a mathematical theory’s silence about a cause is not evidence that there is none — it is a consequence of the method.
summary.deepDive:
Feser’s pairing — quantum theory as **potentiality without actuality**, the block universe as **actuality without potentiality** — is the most illuminating idea in this section.

Causation is an actual thing actualizing a potential. A full causal picture needs both sides. Now look at what each physical picture drops.

- In quantum descriptions of random decay, of particles emerging from the vacuum, of correlated Bell measurements, potentials are being realized — the atom could decay, and it does — but nothing in the formalism is shown *doing* the actualizing. The actualizer side is missing.
- In the block universe everything simply is. Nothing waits to be realized. The potential side is missing.

So neither picture contains causation — and for a methodological reason. A consistently mathematicized description is bound to omit one side or the other. It is the *method* that drains causality out of the picture. To draw metaphysical conclusions from either is to mistake abstractions for concrete realities.

Now the other half: **causation without determinism**. A loaded die lands on six far more often than chance would predict. Its bias explains the pattern and makes any particular six intelligible, without fixing which roll will come up six. Feser’s claim is that this is enough for causation — a cause must make its effect intelligible, not necessitate it. The demand that every cause determine its effect is an assumption imported into the debate, not something the principle of causality says.

**Two errors to name.** Treating ‘random’ as equivalent to ‘uncaused’. And inferring absence in nature from absence in a representation — the same mistake Feser diagnosed in Hume’s stone, in sharper form. Its absence from the representation does not even make it *likely* to be absent from nature, if we already know the representation would leave it out whether or not it is there.

**Step 4**, and **step 1**.

checks.q: What must a cause do to be sufficient to explain its effect, on the Aristotelian view Feser defends?
options: Determine the effect with complete certainty
Precede the effect in time
Make the effect intelligible, even if not deterministically
Be directly observable
checks.explanation: Causality doesn’t entail determinism. A cause need only make its effect intelligible, as even the Copenhagen interpretation allows.

checks.q: What does the ‘colour hold’ analogy suggest about quantum theory?
options: That its own features may hint at the causal potentialities it doesn’t depict
That physics is secretly colourful
That quantum theory is false
That artists understand physics better than physicists
checks.explanation: As the inked lines let you infer contours supplied only by the colour, quantum theory’s potentia-like features hint at Aristotelian potentiality — Heisenberg’s own comparison.

summary.heading: Radioactive decay
summary.plain: A radioactive atom decays at an unpredictable moment — but unpredictable is not uncaused. It decays as it does because of what kind of atom it is; something made it; and something keeps it existing as that kind of atom right now. Phil Dowe’s test: if someone leaves a bucket of radioactive material in your room and you get sick, you rightly hold them responsible — which shows we already treat probabilistic links as causal.
summary.body:
Phil Dowe’s example: an unstable lead-210 atom may decay, without outside interference, into mercury-206, with probability *x* of doing so in the next minute. For the Aristotelian, lead-210 simply behaves according to its **nature**, as copper conducts electricity and a dog chases squirrels — and its nature includes that probability. The decay is not deterministic, but that does not make it unintelligible: it is grounded in what it is to be lead-210 rather than some other kind of thing. That grounding is what Aristotelians call a **formal cause**. There is also an **efficient cause**: whatever originally generated the atom. And — the point that matters most here — a deeper efficient cause in whatever keeps the atom in existence here and now as lead-210, with its nondeterministic tendency, rather than as some other thing or nothing at all. That too presupposes the actualization of a potential, and so an actualizer.

Dowe adds two observations. If he brings a bucket of lead-210 into your room and you get radiation sickness, he is responsible — and one cannot be morally responsible for what one is not causally responsible for, so the indeterministic link must be causal. And scientists describe such decay as the **production** of mercury-206, and ‘production’ is a near-synonym for ‘causation’. The air of paradox comes entirely from conflating deterministic causality with causality as such.
summary.takeaway: Lead-210’s probabilistic decay is grounded in its nature, was made possible by whatever generated it, and depends on whatever sustains it now. Indeterministic is not uncaused; the case shows only that some causal situations are more complicated than others.
summary.deepDive:
How can a thing’s nature ground a **probability** rather than a certainty?

Ask why lead-210 has the decay tendency it has, while other isotopes decay far faster or not at all. The answer is in terms of what lead-210 *is* — its nuclear structure, the kind of thing it is. So there is an explanation. It just isn’t of the form ‘this made it decay at 3:07 p.m.’; it is of the form ‘this kind of thing has this tendency, of this strength’. A person with a quick temper is likelier to snap when provoked, and his temperament genuinely explains why he snaps more often than his calm neighbour, without fixing which provocation will do it. Real, explanatory, and probabilistic.

Then notice that Feser’s analysis **multiplies** the causes rather than eliminating them: the atom’s nature, whatever generated it, and whatever sustains it now. The third is the one the argument needs, and the decay’s indeterminism does not touch it at all — an atom with an indeterministic tendency is still an atom whose existing as such is an actualized potential.

A footnote adds that Dowe himself reads Newton’s first law as saying that a body’s inertia, conceived as a property of the body, *causes* its uniform motion — a parallel John Losee points out, and one that fits the ‘spontaneous’ reading of inertia from two lessons back.

**The error to name:** ‘if we can’t predict when it decays, nothing causes it to decay.’ Unpredictability of timing is not absence of cause; it means the cause is probabilistic.

checks.q: What does Feser identify as the formal cause of lead-210’s decay?
options: Whatever generated the atom
Its nature, what it is to be lead-210
The observer who measures it
The mercury atom that is produced
checks.explanation: The atom’s nature or substantial form grounds its probability of decay. What generated it is the efficient cause, and the mercury is the effect.

checks.q: What is the point of Dowe’s remark that scientists describe decay as the ‘production’ of mercury-206?
options: That mercury is manufactured industrially
That decay is really deterministic after all
That lead is a kind of factory
That ‘production’ is nearly a synonym for causation, so scientists already speak of decay as causal
checks.explanation: The apparent paradox arises only if we fallaciously conflate causality as such with deterministic causality.

summary.heading: Outdated science?
summary.plain: Aristotle got plenty of science wrong — the earth at the centre, the four elements, natural places. But the argument uses his analysis of change, not his physics, and science itself presupposes that change is real. The other version of the objection, that a desk is ‘really’ a cloud of particles, misses the point too: the particles are simply *how* the desk holds up the cup.
summary.body:
The sweeping version says modern science refuted Aristotelianism, so an Aristotelian argument for God is no more relevant than Aristotelian astronomy. But ‘Aristotelianism’ covers an enormous variety of philosophical, scientific, theological and political ideas. Specific **scientific** theses associated with medieval Aristotelianism — geocentrism, the ancient theory of the elements, the notion that objects have natural places — have indeed been refuted. The **metaphysical** thesis that change is the actualization of a potential has not. Indeed, since observation and experiment presuppose the transition from one perceptual experience to another, any possible scientific theory presupposes it.

The narrower version attacks the examples. Arthur Eddington contrasted the solid table of common sense with the physicist’s cloud of particles in mostly empty space: an object does not fall through the table because its particles continuously strike the object’s underside. So (the objection runs) the floor-holds-desk-holds-cup picture gets the science wrong. Feser calls this quite silly, for three reasons. It assumes common sense and the description given by physics are in **competition**, which is controversial at best — the particle details, by themselves, merely supply the **mechanism** by which the desk holds the cup. It is raised **selectively**: nobody quibbles from particle physics when an engineer says how thick a foundation must be, or a doctor explains how a herniated disk fails to support the spine. And the scientific details are **irrelevant** to what the examples were introduced to show — actualization of a potential, and the difference between hierarchical and linear series — notions that apply at any level of description. No one thinks it clever to tell a physicist that photons are too small to ride on.
summary.takeaway: What modern science refuted were specific Aristotelian *scientific* claims, not the metaphysics of act and potency, which science itself presupposes.
summary.deepDive:
How can a metaphysical thesis be *more secure* than a scientific one? Consider what it would take to refute ‘change is the actualization of a potential’ experimentally. You would set up an experiment and observe the result — which means one experience giving way to another, a potential for knowing becoming actual knowing. Any experimental test of the thesis would presuppose the thesis. It is not beyond criticism; it is beyond *experimental* refutation, and can be challenged only philosophically.

Now run Eddington’s own picture through the argument and watch it survive. Suppose the cup and desk really are clouds of particles, with electromagnetic repulsion keeping the cup’s particles at a certain height above the desk’s. Then the cup’s potential to be at that height is actualized by the desk’s particles; their ability to do that depends on their being held in place by the floor’s particles; and so on down. We still have a hierarchical series of actualizers, described more finely. The physics supplies the **mechanism**; it does not abolish the relation.

That is the same formula Feser used about relativity and about inertia: the scientific details affect **how** the concepts apply, never **whether** they apply. It is worth collecting, because it is his standard move against every objection from physics in this chapter — and a reminder that the examples are illustrations, not premises. No numbered step mentions a desk.

checks.q: According to Feser, which of these has modern science refuted?
options: The ancient theory of the elements and the notion of natural places
The thesis that change is the actualization of potential
The principle of causality
The distinction between linear and hierarchical series
checks.explanation: Specific scientific theses associated with medieval Aristotelianism were refuted. The metaphysical theses weren’t — and science presupposes them.

checks.q: What is Feser’s deepest reply to the Eddington-style objection?
options: Eddington was mistaken about particles
Engineers never use physics
The scientific details are irrelevant to the concepts the examples introduce; they affect how, not whether, those concepts apply
Tables are not really made of particles
checks.explanation: The examples only introduce actualization and the linear/hierarchical distinction, which apply whether we describe desks or clouds of particles.

summary.heading: Are hierarchical series real — and why they cannot regress forever
summary.plain: Two last challenges to the all-at-once chain. First: are there really causes acting at the same moment as their effects? Yes — when you push a chair across a room, your pushing and the chair’s being pushed are one event, even though it takes time. Second: why can’t a chain of borrowed power just go on forever? Because borrowers never explain where the power came from. An endless row of mirrors reflecting a face still needs a real face somewhere.
summary.body:
**Are causes ever simultaneous with their effects?** Wouldn’t precision instruments reveal a lag between stick and stone, or between desk and cup? And hasn’t relativity cast doubt on simultaneity anyway? Feser’s replies:

- **Simultaneous does not entail instantaneous.** An event like using a stick to move a stone is spread out through time. To call the motions simultaneous is to say that the stick’s moving the stone and the stone’s being moved by the stick are parts of the same one event, however long it lasts. As Clarke puts it: it takes time to push a chair across a room, but there is no time at all between my pushing the chair and the chair being pushed.
- **Immediate causes are simultaneous with their effects.** Against Hume, Mumford and Anjum argue that it is not ball A’s earlier motion that causes B’s motion — A could have been stopped before it influenced B, and B may or may not roll on regardless. The causing happens at impact, and A’s impacting B and B’s being impacted by A are the same event. Likewise the immediate cause of the broken window is not the throwing of the brick but the brick’s pushing into the glass.
- **This does not collapse history into one instant.** Distinguish causation *within* a process from one process setting up conditions for another: the sugar dissolving in the tea does not cause the drinking of the tea ten minutes later; it results in a set of conditions that the separate process of drinking makes use of.
- **Relativity is irrelevant.** It concerns whether *distinct, spatially separated* events are simultaneous. Here cause and effect are parts of one event at one location.

**And in any case**, what makes a series hierarchical is not simultaneity but derivative power — which is exactly why such a series cannot regress to infinity while a linear one can. Each member of a linear series has its causal power inherently relative to the others, so there is no need to trace any member’s action back to a first. In a hierarchical series every member other than the first can act only insofar as its power to act is imparted from outside. If D is actualized by C only insofar as C is being actualized by B, and B by A, then until we reach something that can actualize without being actualized — something that can impart causal power without having to derive it — we have not explained anything. We have only **passed the explanatory buck**. A hierarchical series without a first member would be an instrument that is not the instrument of anything.

Two objections miss this. **Infinite mathematical series** are no counterexample, because they involve no instrumental and primary causes — indeed no causality at all. Aristotelians accept infinite mathematical series, and generally accept that linear causal series could in principle lack a beginning, which is also why cosmological models of a beginningless universe or multiverse are beside the point. (Feser’s footnote charges Graham Oppy with claiming that Aquinas gives no reason to rule out an infinite series while simply ignoring the role instrumental causality plays in the argument.) And the **question-begging** charge — that calling the other causes ‘instrumental’ already assumes there is a first cause using them — fails, because to characterize a cause as instrumental is merely to say that it derives its causal power from something else. Even a sceptic can grant that a stick cannot move a stone under its own power, whether or not he goes on to agree that the regress terminates.
summary.takeaway: Immediate causes are simultaneous with their effects as parts of one event, which need not be instantaneous — and in any case a hierarchy is defined by derived power, not timing. Derived power cannot be derived from nothing, however long the chain.
summary.deepDive:
**Immediate versus remote causes.** Take the billiard balls slowly. Ball A rolls toward B. Is A’s *rolling* the cause of B’s motion? Not strictly: A could be stopped a centimetre short and have no causal influence on B at all, and after impact B may keep rolling whether or not A is still there. The causing happens only *at impact* — A’s pushing into B and B’s being pushed by A, one event described from two sides, with no gap between them. The brick’s earlier throw is causally relevant to the broken window, and there is a perfectly good sense in which we call it the cause, but the **immediate** cause is the brick pressing into the glass, simultaneous with the glass giving way.

Duration is no obstacle. A potter molds a vase over an hour; throughout that hour the potter’s molding and the clay’s being molded are one ongoing event — simultaneous without being instantaneous. So are a sugar cube dissolving and a heater warming a room.

**Why the regress must end.** Suppose there were derivers all the way down. Where does the power come from? Each member has it only by receiving it, and each one it receives from has it only by receiving it too. However far you go, you never reach anything that *has* the power to give. So nothing in the series has any power to pass along — which contradicts the supposition that its members are actually acting. Feser’s mirror image fixes this: mirror reflects mirror reflects mirror, forever. Even granting the infinity, the image is of a *face*, and some actual face must be the source of the content being reflected. What cannot exist is only mirror images and never any face.

**Why that is not question-begging.** Sobel’s worry is that an ‘instrument’ is always the instrument *of* someone, so calling the intermediate causes instruments already assumes a first cause. Feser’s reply is that the term is defined neutrally: an instrumental cause is one that *derives its causal power from something else*, and that says nothing about whether the derivations end. A sceptic can accept the definition and still ask ‘why not derivers all the way down?’ — at which point the mirror argument is offered as an answer, not smuggled in as a definition.

**The Al–Bob–Chuck footnote, precisely.** Members of a linear series have causal power inherently *relative to one another*: Bob can beget Chuck whether or not Al is alive, and it is Bob who begets Chuck, not Al using Bob as an instrument. They do not have it inherently *full stop*. None of them could beget, or do anything else, for an instant unless the potential of the atoms making up his body to constitute a living body were being actualized here and now — which is in nobody’s power. So every stage of a linear series presupposes hierarchical series.

**Two misconceptions.** That Aristotelians think infinity is impossible — they do not; the need for a first member has nothing to do with a horror of infinity and everything to do with the nature of derived power. And that ‘simultaneous causation’ means everything happens at once, or that relativity has abolished simultaneity as such.

This is the full defence of **step 11**, and it also protects **steps 7–10**, which speak of *concurrent* actualizers.

checks.q: What does Feser say about the relation between ‘simultaneous’ and ‘instantaneous’?
options: They mean the same thing
A cause and its effect can be simultaneous as parts of one event that lasts through time
Simultaneous causes must be instantaneous
Only instantaneous events are causal
checks.explanation: Pushing a chair across a room takes time, but the pushing and the being-pushed are one event, with no time between them.

checks.q: Why do infinite mathematical series fail as counterexamples to Feser’s claim?
options: Infinite mathematical series don’t exist
They are actually finite
They involve no instrumental and primary causes — indeed no causation at all
Mathematicians disagree about them
checks.explanation: What must have a first member is a series of derived causal power. Numbers pass along no power, so they are irrelevant. Aristotelians accept infinite series happily.

checks.q: In the Al–Bob–Chuck example, in what sense does each man have causal power inherently?
options: Relative to the other members of the linear series: Bob can beget Chuck whether or not Al is alive
Absolutely and without qualification
Only derivatively, through Al
In no sense at all
checks.explanation: Their begetting isn’t instrumental the way a stick’s pushing is. But none has inherent power full stop, since each depends at every instant on hierarchical series sustaining his body.

summary.heading: Why an unmovable mover?
summary.plain: Could the first cause be something that merely happens to have some unused ‘can be’s? No. Anything whose existence depended on a ‘can be’ being made real would need a further cause, and so would not be first. And the objection that a cause must change in order to act? The causes we know change because they are limited — an arm is here and only potentially there. Remove the limits and the reason for changing goes with them.
summary.body:
Grant an **unmoved** mover; must it be **unmovable** — purely actual? Why not a first actualizer with potentialities that simply are not being actualized, at least while it is functioning as first cause? If it had any, it would not have unity, immateriality, eternity, perfection or omnipotence.

Feser’s answer begins by recalling what the regress is a regress of: actualizers **of the existence of things**. Suppose the first actualizer had some potentiality that had to be actualized in order for it to exist. What actualizes it?

- **Something other than itself** — then the so-called first actualizer is not the first after all; that further thing is, or something beyond it.
- **A purely actual part of it** — then that part is the true first actualizer, and the merely potential ‘part’ is not really part of it at all but merely the first of its effects.
- **A part that is itself a mixture of act and potency** — then what actualizes *that* part’s potentialities? Some further mixed part? Then we are back in a vicious regress and have not reached a first actualizer at all.

So no sense can be made of a first actualizer of the existence of things that is not purely actual.

Then the last objection: isn’t the very notion of a purely actual actualizer **incoherent**, since to actualize something is to change? Three replies. It **begs the question** — if the premises are true and the conclusion follows, the conclusion is true and therefore coherent, so the critic must show that a premise is false or that the inference fails, not simply insist the conclusion is impossible. It commits a **fallacy of accident** — the causes in our experience do change as they act, but that no more shows all causes must than the fact that every U.S. president has been under seven feet tall shows that no seven-footer could ever become president. And the notion is not paradoxical the way ‘immortal mortal’ is; the causes we know have to be actualized as they act precisely because they are **limited** — an arm is actually at one point in space and only potentially at another — and something devoid of all potentiality has no such limitation.
summary.takeaway: A first actualizer with any potential would itself need actualizing, so the only coherent first actualizer is purely actual. The changes we see in familiar causes reflect their limitations, not anything in the nature of causing.
summary.deepDive:
**The three-way dilemma, with a candidate in hand.** Suppose someone proposes X as the first actualizer of the existence of things, and grants that X has some potential P that must be actualized for X to exist. Ask what actualizes P.

- **Something outside X — call it Y.** Then X’s existence depends on Y, and Y (or something beyond Y) is the first actualizer. The proposal defeats itself.
- **A purely actual part of X — call it X-1.** Then X-1 actualizes everything, including the rest of X, without being actualized. X-1 is the real first actualizer, and the potential ‘part’ of X is simply its first effect. We have arrived at pure actuality anyway.
- **A part of X that mixes act and potency — call it X-2.** Then X-2’s own potentials need actualizing. By what? Another mixed part? The regress is running again, with no first actualizer in sight.

No option leaves a first actualizer that is not purely actual. So if there is a first actualizer at all — and Stage 1 argued that there must be — it is **pure act**, and everything derived in Stage 2 follows.

**Why familiar causes change as they act.** Your arm is actually *here* and only potentially *there*. To get the stick *there*, the arm’s own potential to be there has to be actualized by something else. The change is required because the arm is limited — located, partial, extended. Remove every limitation and the reason for being actualized while acting disappears with it. Generalizing from limited causes to all causes is precisely the **fallacy of accident**: reasoning from an accidental feature of the examples to a necessary feature of the kind.

Feser’s first reply is methodological and worth keeping. ‘Your conclusion is incoherent’ is not an objection to an argument; it is a refusal of one. If the premises are true and the logic valid, the conclusion is true and therefore coherent — so the critic owes us a false premise or a broken inference.

**The phrase to read carefully:** ‘unmoved mover’ does not mean ‘a mover that happens to be at rest just now’. The conclusion is a mover that *could not* be moved.

This secures the passage from ‘first’ to ‘purely actual’ in **steps 12–14**, and with it the premise Stage 2 leans on throughout (**steps 16, 20, 28, 31**) that pure act has no potentials.

checks.q: If the supposed first actualizer had a potential that something other than itself actualizes, what follows?
options: It would not really be the first actualizer
It would be self-caused
There would be two gods
Nothing important follows
checks.explanation: The external actualizer, or something beyond it, would then be first. That is the first horn of Feser’s dilemma.

checks.q: Why does Feser say ‘immortal mortal’ is unlike ‘purely actual actualizer’?
options: Both phrases are self-contradictory
Neither phrase is contradictory
Mortality is a kind of potential
‘Immortal mortal’ is self-contradictory, while ‘something that actualizes without being actualized’ is not
checks.explanation: An immortal mortal would both die and not die. A purely actual actualizer involves no such contradiction, so the charge of incoherence needs an actual argument.

checks.q: Why, according to Feser, do the actualizers we experience change as they act?
options: Because causation as such requires change
Because they are limited: an arm is actually here and only potentially there
Because of entropy
Because they are alive
checks.explanation: Their limitations explain why they must be actualized while acting. Pure actuality has no such limits, so ‘all causes change’ is a fallacy of accident.

merged: Old 11 (Perfection and goodness) + old 12 (Unity) -> 'Perfection, goodness and unity'. The unity argument just IS the perfection argument applied to counting: any feature distinguishing two purely actual beings would be a perfection one has and the other lacks, i.e. a privation. Splitting them forced the second lesson to re-derive privation before it could start. 1,422 words -> 934.

Old 18 (beginnings and wholes) + old 19 ('What caused God?') -> 'Three misreadings: a beginning, the whole universe, and What caused God?'. All three objections make the same mistake — attacking a premise the argument does not have — and all three sit under Feser's single 'Common misunderstandings' heading. 1,411 words -> 930.

Old 27 (Are hierarchical causal series real?) + old 28 (Why a hierarchical regress can't be infinite) -> one lesson. These are one section in Feser, and they overlapped badly: old 27's closing point (what defines a hierarchical series is derivative power, not simultaneity) was old 28's opening thesis, stated twice. Merging removed the duplication and let the regress argument — the chapter's hardest single move — grow: the mirror image, the 'derivers all the way down' reductio, and the Sobel reply are each unpacked properly. 1,430 words -> 1,272.

NOT merged: the Stage 2 attribute lessons (old 10, 13–16; new 10, 12–15). They looked like a fragmented derivation but are not one: the negative attributes run off 'no potency', omnipotence runs off the Stage 1 regress result, and intelligence needs two independent preliminaries (what intellect is, and proportionate causality) before it can be derived. Feser's own order is account-of-intelligence -> PPC -> derivation, and collapsing it would have compressed exactly the derivation you asked to expand. They were trimmed instead.
errors_fixed: Old lesson 22 (Newton on inertia), plain: 'Newton's law says a moving object keeps moving unless something stops it.' Wrong twice over — the law is that a body in motion remains in motion unless acted upon by OUTSIDE FORCES (a force can also accelerate or deflect it, not just stop it), and the motion described is uniform straight-line motion. Now: 'a body in motion stays in motion unless an outside force acts on it', with the body keeping Feser's own wording.

Old lesson 28, body: attributed the 'infinite mathematical series' counterexample to Graham Oppy ('**Infinite mathematical series** (Graham Oppy)'). Feser's main text raises that counterexample generically; his footnote cites Oppy only for the different claim that Aquinas gives no reason to rule out an infinite series, and answers that Oppy ignores the role of instrumental causality. Now stated generically, with Oppy's actual objection and Feser's actual reply in a parenthesis. (Note: the parallel keyTerms/quiz audit running in this session found the same misattribution in the quiz and flashcards — it is systemic, not local.)

Old lesson 17 (formal statement), body: listed the load-bearing Stage 1 premises as 'steps 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 10 and 11', omitting step 6 ('The occurrence of any change C presupposes some thing or substance S which changes'). Step 6 is a premise, and it is the hinge of the whole change->existence pivot: without it you never get from a change to the changing thing's existence. Added.

Old lesson 12 (Unity), deepDive: gave 'Material and temporal features ... are unavailable, because pure actuality is immaterial and eternal (steps 23–25)' as a ground for unity. In the formal statement unity is steps 15–18, derived BEFORE immateriality (25) and eternity (23), so as written the bullet cites later steps to support an earlier one. The old text flagged the compression in a nuance further down but left the circular-looking bullet standing. Now stated once and cleanly: the informal argument appeals to immateriality and eternity, while the formal version places unity first and rests on the single premise that any differentiating feature would require an unactualized potential.

Old lesson 4, plain: 'the book admits that such a chain could go back forever'. 'Admits' reads as conceding a fact. Feser grants an infinite past FOR THE SAKE OF ARGUMENT and calls the pre-Big-Bang/multiverse speculation 'all very dubious'. Changed to 'grants — for the sake of argument — that such a chain could run back forever', and the body now says he calls the speculation dubious and then sets it aside as irrelevant either way.

Old lesson 5, plain: 'Take away the floor and everything above it falls instantly.' Feser says that if the floor collapses the desk goes with it and the cup falls as a result — what ceases instantly is the HOLDING, not the falling.
